arxiv-2511-20039:
Bobrowski and Pilipenko catalog every random walk that can live on a star-shaped network. Their 2025 paper describes Brownian motions on infinite star graphs. A star graph joins several half-lines at one center. Away from the center, motion looks like ordinary Brownian wandering. What happens at the junction decides each process's character.

The authors give a full analytic and stochastic description. All Feller processes of this kind are classified. Boundary behavior at the center is parameterized explicitly. The work continues Itô and McKean's classic half-line study. Multi-armed bandit theory supplies a fresh viewpoint here. Generators and their domains are characterized in detail. Feller and Wentzell boundary conditions frame the analysis. Processes may stick, reflect, or jump at the center. Each admissible rule yields a genuine process. The classification covers stars with finitely many arms.
arxiv-2511-20239:
Krejčí, Kost, Xia, Svensson, and Straka teach trackers to expect objects to hide each other. Their 2025 paper handles occlusion in multi-object tracking. Sensors need line of sight to spot anything. Objects in front block those behind them. Trackers that ignore this lose hidden objects entirely.

The standard detection model assumes a fixed spotting chance. Their upgrade makes detection probability depend on all objects present. Each object gets an expected probability of detection. The expectation conditions on that object existing. It uses the reduced Palm density from point process theory. Visibility is judged relative to the sensor and the crowd. Uncertainties about every object enter one clear formula. A multi-Bernoulli mixture filter with marks implements it. Visual tracking tests showed the strategy beating rivals. Safety uses like driving and naval watch motivate the care. The method stays fully model-based throughout.
arxiv-2511-20639:
Zou, Yang, Qiu, and a large team let AI agents collaborate inside their hidden states. Their 2025 paper presents LatentMAS for multi-agent language model systems. Agent teams normally talk through text messages to each other. Text channels lose information and burn tokens heavily. Latent space offers a richer shared medium.

Each agent generates latent thoughts as final-layer hidden states. A shared latent workspace stores and passes those states. Nothing is lost in translation between agents this way. Theory shows higher expressiveness than text-based teamwork. Complexity drops substantially at the same time, they prove. Nine benchmarks covered math, science, commonsense, and code tasks. Accuracy rose by up to 14.6 percent over strong baselines. Output token use fell by seventy to eighty-four percent. End-to-end runs finished about four times faster. The framework needs no extra training at all. Hierarchical team layouts showed the clearest gains.
arxiv-2511-20739:
Oem Trivedi and Venkat Venkatasubramanian propose in 2025 a game-based retelling of cosmology. The standard picture leans on unknowns. About 95 percent of the universe's energy budget is dark energy and dark matter, whose nature nobody knows. Measurements also quarrel over the Hubble constant and the clumpiness measure S8. Cosmological Teleodynamics replaces new particles with memory: the universe's past organisation biases what happens next.

The approach, borrowed from goal-driven agent theory, weights cosmic histories and adds a bias term for memory. From that they derive the Friedmann, Boltzmann, and Poisson equations with the memory built in. The equations yield dark-energy-like acceleration and dark-matter-like clustering without either substance, plus growth suppression, halo signatures tied to environment, and lopsided velocity fields that particle dark matter cannot produce. Its capstone, a Law of Universal Arbitrage Equilibrium, has the universe expanding toward a Nash equilibrium, like a potential game.
arxiv-2511-20939:
Youhong Chen and colleagues show in 2025 how a data-driven method can find the culprit behind a real power-grid oscillation in Denmark. Unwanted oscillations can shake a grid, and blaming the right plant matters. Their tool, Extended Dynamic Mode Decomposition, grows out of Koopman operator theory, which rewrites nonlinear dynamics in a linear form. It needed no model of the Danish grid.

The team fed it only voltage and current phasor recordings from nineteen measurement units at different voltage levels, a blind test. The method pinpointed the plant behind the oscillation, matching the inverter-based plant that grid operator Energinet later confirmed, where a control-system fault was the root cause. The conventional dissipating energy flow method, used in an established industry tool, failed to identify that plant clearly. The authors argue blind, measurement-only analysis can target mitigation at the true source instead of the loudest symptom.
arxiv-2511-21039:
Naoki Okamoto and colleagues probe in 2025 an exotic ordered state in the compound PrIr2Zn20, where the ordering involves not magnetic poles but quadrupoles, the shape of electron clouds around praseodymium ions. The material is a non-Kramers system, so ordinary magnetism is absent and these higher-order arrangements rule its low-temperature behaviour. It enters an antiferroquadrupolar phase below 0.125 kelvin and superconducts below 0.05 kelvin.

The team measured magnetostriction and thermal expansion, tiny length changes, while rotating the magnetic field direction. With the field along the crystal's [001] axis, thermal expansion showed two distinct anomalies, backing earlier reports of an intermediate A phase. Along the [110] axis that phase is absent, a strong directional dependence. Comparing with theory, they find the O20 quadrupole component couples anisotropically and plays the key role in stabilising the A phase. The message: in such systems, simply rotating a field can switch ordered states on and off.
arxiv-2511-21239:
V. Humlová reports first results from the ALICE Collaboration in 2025 on how gluons, the particles gluing atomic nuclei together, behave at extreme energies. In lead-lead collisions at the LHC, a photon from one nucleus can strike the other and create a J/psi particle, a reaction that directly maps the gluon density inside. ALICE covers photon-nucleon energies from 20 to 800 GeV, reaching gluon momentum fractions a thousand times smaller than older experiments.

Humlová presents the energy dependence of coherent production, where the nucleus stays intact and the signal reflects average gluon density. The coherent rate is strongly suppressed at high energies, matching expectations from nuclear shadowing and gluon saturation, where gluons crowd until splitting and merging balance out. For incoherent production, where the nucleus breaks, the momentum-transfer pattern is shallower than nucleon-level models predict, pointing to gluon clumping at scales smaller than a single nucleon.
arxiv-2511-21339:
Tae-Min Choi and eight coauthors build a shared exam for AI assistants that watch surgery, in 2025. Multimodal language models could one day narrate an operation's stage, outline instruments, and answer a surgeon's questions mid-procedure. Existing surgical datasets, though, mostly use question-answer formats with mismatched label schemes and no pixel-level outlines, so models cannot be compared fairly or trained to point at what they describe.

Choi and his coauthors unify laparoscopic, robot-assisted, and micro-surgical data under one taxonomy in SurgMLLMBench. The benchmark pairs workflow labels, stage, phase, and step, alongside pixel-level masks marking each instrument. It adds MAVIS, a new dataset of micro-surgical artificial blood-vessel stitching. Baseline experiments show one model trained on the benchmark performs consistently across all three domains, grounds its answers in accurate masks, and transfers effectively to datasets it never trained on.
arxiv-2511-21739:
Ana Trišović and three coauthors present the first large-scale measurement of how scientists actually use AI foundation models, in 2025. Rather than counting citations or keywords, the team traced real model usage across the scientific literature. Adoption, they find, has grown at nearly exponential rates.

Uptake is highest in Linguistics, Computer Science, and Engineering alike. Vision models see the widest use in science, though language models' share is climbing, and open-weight models dominate. A striking gap concerns size. Builders keep releasing bigger models, and scientists follow far behind: in 2013 the median model built was 7.7 times larger than the median one scientists adopted, and by 2024 that gap had jumped to 26 times. The paper also reports suggestive evidence that this caution costs impact. Papers using larger models appear in higher-impact journals and collect more citations, hinting that scientists may not be harvesting the full benefit of modern AI.
arxiv-2511-21839:
Qiang and colleagues build a small software module that makes physics simulations differentiable, meaning it reports not just results but how they change if each input is nudged. Derivatives show sensitivity and feed gradient-based optimization toward better designs. Their module works by adding a new data type that carries derivatives along through ordinary calculations, so programmers barely change their code at all.

The module is written in five programming languages, Fortran, C++, Java, Python, and Julia, in only a few hundred lines of code, so existing programs can adopt it without rewriting their formulas. As a demonstration, they plugged it into a parallel particle-in-cell code simulating many charged particles across distributed computers via MPI. The combined code could analyse how final beam properties, such as emittance, depend on accelerator settings including space-charge effects, and optimize the accelerator lattice directly from those gradients.
arxiv-2512-00239:
Self-supervised learning lets models train on unlabeled recordings, which is vital for medical time series. Yenho Chen, Maxwell Xu, James Rehg, and Christopher Rozell study representations of physiological signals in 2025. Success depends on keeping information about the body's state while filtering out unrelated noise.

Existing strategies lean on heuristic principles or weakly constrained generative tasks, which can blur exactly the signals clinicians care about. The authors frame pretraining objectives around dynamical systems, the mathematics of systems that evolve over time. Better representations could improve monitoring tools that learn from heart, brain, and breathing data with few labeled examples. Physiological signals, from heartbeats to brain waves, are exactly the data this work targets.
arxiv-2512-00339:
Two species competing across a landscape of connected habitat patches face a strategic choice at every boundary. Kuiyue Liu and Shanshan Chen study the global dynamics of a reaction-diffusion competition model with edge behavior in 2025. The landscape consists of finitely many adjacent patches.

In the two-patch case, edge behavior at the interface can be treated as a strategy. Earlier work showed an ideal free distribution strategy that is globally evolutionarily stable. Knowing when competitors settle into such distributions helps ecologists predict how species sort across fragmented habitats. Edge behavior captures what individuals do at a boundary, where many contests are decided. Global dynamics ask where the whole system ends up, not just where it starts. For folks who tend wild lands cut into small plots, the gain is a clue to where each kind will settle. It shows which plot lines will be the front lines.
arxiv-2512-00639:
Thyroid nodules are common, and telling benign from malignant ones early guides treatment. Mahmoud El Hussieni presents a Doppler-enhanced deep learning approach to thyroid nodule segmentation in 2025, using YOLOv5 instance segmentation on ultrasound images. Rising thyroid cancer prevalence has spurred computer-aided detection methods.

Accurate segmentation of nodules is a critical first step toward AI-assisted clinical decision support. Doppler imaging adds blood-flow information that ordinary ultrasound lacks, which may sharpen the nodule boundaries the model must find. Better segmentation supports radiologists measuring and tracking nodules across visits. Instance segmentation draws each nodule separately, not just a category mask. Ultrasound is cheap and radiation-free, which is why better analysis of it matters. For scan teams, the gain is time. A tool that draws each lump with care can cut the hours spent on marks, and leave more hours for hard calls.
arxiv-2512-00739:
Diyu Shen and five coauthors review intense electromagnetic fields in heavy-ion collisions in a 2025 paper. In such collisions, atomic nuclei crash at nearly the speed of light. The crash dumps huge energy into a small region and heats it until hadrons melt into free quarks and gluons.

The speeding nuclei also carry very strong electric and magnetic fields. The review gathers theory predictions about those fields and the experimental results that test them. Fields this strong may change how particles form and move in the hot aftermath. The summary gives researchers a shared map of what is known and what is still open.
arxiv-2512-01239:
Sohail Farhangi and Bill Mance study what makes a number normal in odd base systems. A normal number uses each digit block as often as chance would say. That trait is well known for plain base counts. It has also been shown for many other ways to write numbers.

The pair turn to Cantor series, where the base can change at each step. A rule that shifts as it goes can make the series on the fly. They build the theory of normal form for that case. The work links digit traits to the rule that made the series.
arxiv-2512-01339:
Xiaojun Zhang and co-authors study bound states that hide inside a spread of free states. Such states are known in single-particle physics. Their kin for pairs of parts are far less known. Pairs that stick as one unit are called doublons.

The team finds a bound state set inside the doublon spread. It forms when four atoms link to a chain of linked rings with strong on-site push. They map how the state acts and holds. Such states could help move quantum states from place to place with less loss, a key need for quantum tools.
arxiv-2512-01439:
Bharatdeep Hazarika and co-authors build a chat aid for finance in many tongues. India has dozens of major tongues and many more minor ones. Just a small share of users grasp English well. That gap blocks access to bank and payment apps.

Their system talks with users in their own tongue. It aims to guide tasks like payments and balance checks by voice and text. Talks in a home tongue build trust for first-time users. Work like this can widen fair access to digital finance across India. Voice-first design is central, since many first-time users read little in any tongue and learn apps best by hearing steps spoken aloud.
arxiv-2512-01539:
Connor Roberts and Gunnar Pruessner give exact results for active crystals in a harmonic model. Active particles like cells can form near-crystal lattices. Those lattices play core roles in living systems. Past theory leaned on the simple one-dimensional case too much.

The pair compute where the harmonic model breaks down. Instabilities show which crystal traits it can and cannot predict. Their results link measurable traits to model terms. That link helps biologists read cell lattice data with the right caveats about model limits. Exact results also mark where the harmonic picture first fails, so later nonlinear work knows the precise point where it must take over.
arxiv-2512-01639:
Conor Rosato and co-authors improve outbreak detection when data arrives out of order. Particle filters estimate hidden epidemic states well. Real reports often land late or out of sequence. That disorder can throw off a filter's state.

Their method adds Markov-switching regimes for endemic and outbreak phases. A fixed-lag particle filter handles the late data. Regime switches let the model jump modes as an outbreak starts. Earlier, cleaner detection helps health teams act while spread is still small. Out-of-sequence handling is built in, not patched on, which matters when labs report cases days late during a fast-moving outbreak.
arxiv-2512-02039:
Logicians extend first-order logic by letting formulas consult an ordering of nearby elements, as long as the answer does not depend on which ordering was picked. Derek Aoki's 2025 paper studies this local-order-invariant logic on classes of structures whose connections stay bounded in degree.

The questions trace back to work by Weinstein about how much extra power order-invariance buys, on bounded-degree structures, on finite structures generally, and on locally finite ones. Expressive power questions decide what properties computers can even state, let alone check, about networks and data. Aoki's results map where this polite fiction of an ordering actually adds strength.
arxiv-2512-02239:
A particle can start in one pure quantum state. Once it trades energy with its surroundings, it is best seen as a mix of states. Each state in the mix has its own chance of showing up. Arsam Najafian and Mark Van Raamsdonk compute in 2025 how that mix shifts during simple two-particle collisions.

They track the mix with math: a reduced density operator lists the states, and its weights give their odds. With numeric work in one and two space dimensions, they show how both the states and the weights move with time. Watching the mix grow, hit by hit, clarifies how pure quantum states decay into mixed ones.
arxiv-2512-02339:
Tell apart two nearly identical objects in a video and the eye uses motion, not appearance. Chenshuang Zhang and five co-authors report in 2025 that pre-trained video diffusion models have quietly learned exactly that skill, tracking similar-looking objects without any supervision or task-specific training.

Supervised trackers perform well but need labeled data, while self-supervised ones falter when visual cues become ambiguous. The diffusion models' internal motion representations turn out to be strong enough to track by movement alone. The finding suggests generative video models absorb physical understanding as a by-product, a resource other vision tasks may be able to borrow.
arxiv-2512-02439:
Allah Ditta and six co-authors build a model of a charged compact star, a dense object held up by strong gravity. Their 2025 study works inside a changed form of gravity that mixes symmetric teleparallel ideas with the Euler-Heisenberg view of electric fields. The star matter pushes out unevenly in different directions.

Inside the model, the team uses the MIT bag model, a standard way to describe quark matter. They link key parts of the model and reach an exact solution of the field equations. The work also checks mass and radius stability for such stars. Work like this helps map which stars can exist and which would soon fall apart.
arxiv-2512-02539:
Dongmin Kim and co-authors tackle a bottleneck in fault tolerant quantum computing: too few decoders. Quantum error correction produces a stream of syndrome data that decoders have to read fast and well. In large systems, logical qubits far outnumber the decoders on hand, so scheduling becomes a core problem.

Their constraint optimal approach allocates decoder time where it helps most, under strict limits. Good allocation keeps errors from piling up while hardware stays scarce. As quantum machines grow, smart sharing of decoding power may matter as much as the decoders themselves for keeping computations reliable. More qubits will need this kind of smart time share if they are to work as one machine at all.
arxiv-2512-02639:
Lisa Schraut-May and eleven co-authors study crystals of zinc-phthalocyanine, a light absorbing molecule. In a molecular crystal, light excites pairs of neighboring molecules together, an effect called excitonic coupling. That coupling is very sensitive to how neighbors sit, tilt, and overlap.

Small changes in packing can mimic the signs of a phase transition in optical spectra. The team traces such mimicked transitions to competing couplings between molecules. Knowing the true cause prevents false claims of new phases, and helps design organic materials whose light response is tuned on purpose. Packing rules learned here feed the design of dyes and films that drink light for work in cells.
arxiv-2512-02939:
Tanay Kumar, Hongying Zhao, and Xuehua Zhang dry thick slurry waste faster by joining two transport tricks. Concentrated slurry dries slowly because water hides between particles and escapes poorly. Their sailboat evaporator uses a root like structure for wind assisted interfacial evaporation.

Pendular water transport pulls liquid through bridges between particles toward the surface. Wind then carries the vapor away at the interface. Combining both paths attacks the drying bottleneck from inside and outside. Faster dewatering could cut the volume of industrial and treatment waste that must be hauled away. Dry waste weighs less and hauls for less. A dryer that works on thick goo pays its way in truck trips saved each month of use.
arxiv-2512-03039:
Chen-Hsuan Hsu, Jelena Klinovaja, and Daniel Loss survey helical liquids, unusual one dimensional electron states at material edges. These liquids appear at the boundaries of time reversal invariant topological materials. Their electrons move with spin locked to direction, a property prized for quantum devices.

Progress has stalled on several key challenges, which the authors highlight. They advocate deeper theory of the many body aspects of these systems. Better understanding could stabilize topological zero modes, the building blocks proposed for fault tolerant quantum computation and low loss electronics. Edge states with locked spin are a prize for low loss gear. A clear list of what blocks them is a list worth years of work to get right.
arxiv-2512-03139:
Dark energy may not stay fixed over cosmic time. Eric Linder studies one idea for that change in this 2025 work. Data suggest the dark energy strength may have crossed a key line, called the phantom divide.

Modified gravity, in the Horndeski form, offers one way to explain the crossing. Linder stresses that growth of cosmic structure and lensing must be checked too, not just expansion history. A model that fits all tests at once is far more convincing. The work helps guide how future sky surveys test dark energy ideas. Growth and lensing data will judge the model alongside the expansion history it predicts.
arxiv-2512-03239:
A distant red galaxy, split in two by gravity, gets a close look. Josephine Baggen, Pieter van Dokkum, Ivo Labbé, and Gabriel Brammer study it in this 2025 work. The galaxy is a Little Red Dot seen as it was when the universe was young.

The galaxy cluster Abell 383 lenses it into two images, observed with the Webb telescope. The source shows the class's V-shaped spectrum and a strong Balmer break. Lensing magnifies faint details that would else be lost. The case helps test what Little Red Dots really are. Lensing magnification acts like a natural telescope, enlarging this distant red source.
arxiv-2512-03539:
Holographic microscopes can image cells without labels, but focusing is hard. Hasan Berkay Abdioğlu and co-authors build an automation framework in this 2025 work. Manual operation for repetitive cell tasks wastes expert time and invites human error.

Digital holographic images are noisy and low in contrast. That makes autofocus and object detection tough for standard tools. The authors add real-time control and automation for acousto-holographic microscopy. Automated microscopes could speed cell biology labs and make results more consistent across users. Acousto-holographic control adds sound-based focusing to the imaging, widening what automation must handle in live cell experiments and assays.
arxiv-2512-03839:
Flood models are usually written for specialists, leaving the public and local officials to decode technical output during a crisis. Weilian Li and colleagues propose a different delivery route in a 2025 computational engineering preprint: a three-dimensional virtual geographic environment for flood representation. Their pipeline joins flood modelling, parallel computation, and 3D visualisation in one system for risk communication.

The team tested the approach on a stretch of the Rhine River near Bonn in Germany, building an interactive scene with three-dimensional city models. The whole run finished within a few hours, helped by parallel speedup. Participants without flood experience found the moving, spatial picture easier to grasp than charts or tables. The system can also plug into a cloud platform for intelligent flood management. The authors argue that shared visual understanding helps stakeholders respond more effectively when waters rise.
arxiv-2512-04039:
Generative models that transform simple noise into images, called normalizing flows, are elegant but often slow. Sandeep Nagar's doctoral thesis, presented in this 2025 preprint, attacks that inefficiency and then puts such models to work on practical vision problems. The work falls into two halves: faster flows, and applications ranging from farm produce to art restoration.

The first half contributes six innovations. They include invertible three-by-three convolution layers with proven invertibility conditions, a more efficient coupling layer, and fast algorithms for inverting convolutions. A compact super-resolution model reuses pretrained weights to shrink parameter counts. The second half applies the tools widely. It grades agricultural produce with conditional GANs, maps geology with stacked autoencoders, and hides faces and licence plates in driving datasets through inpainting. A diffusion model adapted for art restoration closes the thesis.
arxiv-2512-04139:
Placing N chess queens on an N-by-N board so none attacks another is a classic puzzle for testing search algorithms. Susmita Sharma and colleagues propose a faster stochastic solver in a 2025 preprint. Exact backtracking always finds a solution but scales terribly. The randomised Las Vegas approach is quick yet erratic, because blind placement wastes effort on doomed arrangements.

Their hybrid keeps the Las Vegas framework but prunes as it goes, dynamically eliminating placements that are already invalid during the random assignment phase. The shrinking search space steadies the algorithm's performance and shortens the hunt. The method consistently produced valid solutions faster than backtracking, which degraded sharply as board size grew. Some variability remains at large sizes, but the trade-off between cost and reliability suits settings where one timely solution matters more than guaranteed completeness, such as resource-constrained systems.
arxiv-2512-04239:
Many industrial plants run best in a repeating cycle, not at a fixed setpoint, when prices or weather keep shifting. Filippo Badalamenti and co-authors design a robust controller for cyclic work in a 2025 preprint on systems and control. The plants are not known in full: each is a mix of a few affine systems, plus noise.

The method works with tubes, bands of states built as polytopes with a fixed shape. It steers the plant along the cyclic path that best fits a stated cost goal. Extra variables keep the plan valid and all limits met, even when the goal is swapped online. If the goal stays put, the plan settles onto the best such tube. A square-cost shortcut recasts the maths as a quadratic program, at far less computing cost. A test case and an eight-state ball-plate rig show it works and scales.
arxiv-2512-04439:
Amin Masoumi and Mert Korkali blend quantum circuits with deep reinforcement learning to keep power grid frequency steady. Grid frequency must hold near its target for the system to stay reliable. Classic feedback controllers use fixed gains, so their accuracy fades as conditions shift. Learning-based controllers adapt, but they demand heavy compute. Their 2025 arXiv paper explores whether a quantum circuit can sharpen that learning.

The design places a quantum circuit and a trial wave pattern inside a deep deterministic policy method. The quantum part helps the agent weigh actions for frequency control tasks. The authors frame the setup for near-term quantum devices, which are small and noisy. They link active controller design with quantum algorithm choices to make the most of scarce hardware. If the gains hold, such hybrid controllers could help grids absorb more wind and solar power without losing stability.
arxiv-2512-04639:
Saumya Chauhan, Mila Hong, and Maria Vazhaeparambil present the first large-scale study of how fake and AI-made images spread through Reddit repost chains. Text misinformation has drawn most research attention so far. Visual content may drive sharing just as much, yet its paths were unmapped. Their 2025 arXiv paper follows image cascades across five Reddit communities with distinct political leanings.

The team blends three signal kinds: the sentiment of post text, visual traits of the images, and spread metrics such as time to first repost and community reach. Their framework predicts near-term virality of single posts with solid accuracy. It predicts long-term cascade spread with striking accuracy. The findings show which image traits and early signals mark a cascade worth watching. Moderators could use such signals to slow synthetic and misleading pictures before they flood a community.
arxiv-2512-04839:
Tianji Cai, Aditya Bhargava, and Benjamin Nachman introduce optimal transport as a physics-based lens for hunting anomalies in particle collision data. Anomaly detection at the Large Hadron Collider searches for events that fit no known process, with only weak guidance about what new physics might look like. Raw low-level data overwhelm simple learners when signals are rare. Their 2025 arXiv paper inserts a structured middle layer: each event is recast by how much work it takes to morph one particle pattern into another.

On the LHC Olympics benchmark, with resonant signals injected at a tiny rate, the transport-based features nearly doubled the significance gain of standard high-level observables. End-to-end deep learning on raw momenta did worse in this faint-signal regime. The gains held across signal kinds and classifiers. Physics-shaped representations may be the boost weak supervision needs.
arxiv-2512-05139:
Yang Xiang and five co-authors present a generative method for sharpening weather data across space and time. Climate reanalyses offer long records but at coarse resolution, while the simulations that exposure studies want cover only short periods. The team's framework first trains a small network on the long coarse record to learn how patterns evolve. It then transfers its knowledge into a larger diffusion-based model that paints in fine detail.

They test the approach by reconstructing a detailed simulation of Asia from a coarser reanalysis, splitting the region and seasons to keep the computation manageable. Statistical checks confirm the two datasets are close enough for the transfer to be safe. The model beats deterministic networks, variational autoencoders, and transfer baselines. Its outputs preserve texture and time correlation. They are good enough to extend the fine record beyond its span, for exposure assessment and environmental monitoring.
arxiv-2512-05239:
Ruofan Gao, Amjed Tahir, Peng Liang, Teo Susnjak, and Foutse Khomh survey what is known about bugs in code written by artificial intelligence. Developers now generate code with AI models at scale, yet those models learned from public code riddled with defects. Reports of flawed output are scattered across the literature with no systematic summary. The authors set out to map the terrain: what kinds of bugs appear, how often, in which models, and what can be done about them.

The survey classifies bug types and patterns in generated code and links them to the models that produced them, giving researchers a reference for comparing claims. It also reviews the fixes and mitigation strategies the literature proposes, from testing regimes to repair techniques. The goal is practical: a shared picture of how AI-generated code fails, so future models improve and their output is assessed with open eyes.
arxiv-2512-05339:
Mahesh Kumar Nandwana and five co-authors introduce Roblox Guard 1.0, a moderation model built to police both what users send to a language model and what it sends back. Post-training alignment alone leaves gaps, so deployed systems need guardrails that generalize to new kinds of harmful content. The model is a fine-tuned mid-sized open model, trained to recognize safety categories it has never seen, organized by an extensible taxonomy.

Training mixed synthetic and open-source safety data, enriched with written reasoning traces and an input-inversion trick that deepens contextual understanding. The authors also release RobloxGuard-Eval, a benchmark with a flexible taxonomy for scoring moderation systems. On out-of-domain safety tests the guard performs strongly. The release is aimed at practitioners who need a guard model that can be retargeted as policies and threats change, rather than frozen to the categories of its training day.
arxiv-2512-05439:
Tarun Suresh, Nalin Wadhwa, Debangshu Banerjee, and Gagandeep Singh present BEAVER, a verifier that gives hard guarantees about what a language model might say. As models move into production, practitioners need to bound the chance of unsafe outputs; sampling a few hundred generations offers intuition but no proof about the tail risks that matter. BEAVER instead explores the model's output space systematically, maintaining provably sound probability bounds on satisfying a stated safety property at every step.

Two new data structures, a token trie and a frontier structure, make that exploration practical. The authors formalize the verification problem, prove the bounds sound, and test the system on four safety properties across a dozen open-weight models. BEAVER flags several times more risky instances than baselines on a tenth of the computing budget, surfacing tail behaviour loose estimates miss. It is a step toward deploying language models with certificates rather than vibes.
arxiv-2512-05539:
Swantje Mahncke, Malte Ott, Lars Reining, and Thomas Wallis build the perfect observer for a classic model of visual clutter. In a dead leaves image, opaque shapes are layered one over another until the frame is covered, mimicking how real scenes occlude. Segmenting such an image is a clean test of perceptual inference. Building on earlier theory, the authors define the model rigorously and derive the Bayesian ideal observer for partitioning small sets of pixels.

The hard part is the prior: how likely each layering arrangement is before any pixel colours are seen, which lifts the observer beyond mere pixel similarity. The exact computations suit only tiny pixel sets, so the paper leans on step-by-step derivations and examples. Tested on many generated datasets, the ideal observer beats prior-only and likelihood-only versions, and all beat chance: a principled ceiling for human and algorithmic segmentation.
arxiv-2512-05639:
Aiman Mushtaq Purra and Danish Rafiq present a way to learn the dynamics of a power grid straight from measurements. As wind and solar feed more power in, grid inertia falls and swings become riskier. Operators need true values for inertia and damping, yet model based estimates scale badly on large networks. Their 2025 method, Latent-SINDy, first compresses the data with singular value decomposition, then fits a sparse model to the compressed signals.

Shrinking the data first curbs overfitting while keeping the core behavior. The framework was checked on test grids, from a modest one up to a large European network with thousands of buses. In each case it recovered the inertia and damping values closely, and the learned models tracked the true dynamics well. Because the models stay readable and cheap to run, the approach suits live monitoring. It could help operators watch stability as renewable shares keep rising.
arxiv-2512-05739:
M Papoutsis and four co-authors revisit how X-rays and ultraviolet light vary together in the active galaxy NGC 5548. A hot corona above its black hole shines in X-rays, while the disk glows in ultraviolet and optical light. Standard theory says disk light echoes the X-rays. Yet rich monitoring data from 2014 show ultraviolet and optical bands moving tightly together, while X-rays correlate only weakly.

The team refits the Hubble and Swift light curves with a corona that changes over time. Its height, spectrum, and power are all allowed to drift. With that freedom, X-ray reverberation explains the ultraviolet variations to within about two percent, and the optical to within about five percent. The fitted corona must reshape itself fast, on timescales of days. The standard picture survives only if the corona is restless, not a steady lamp above the disk.
arxiv-2512-05839:
Basanti Paul, Abhijit Roy, Jagdish Joshi, and Debanjan Bose ask whether two jet firing binaries in our galaxy shine in gamma rays because protons are smashing into stellar wind. The systems, V4641 Sagittarii and SS 433, are microquasars: a star feeding a compact object that answers with relativistic jets. Telescopes have caught them glowing up to peta-electronvolt energies. That makes them candidate PeVatrons.

The team models the hadronic story, in which jet protons strike the companion's wind and spawn gamma rays. Fits pin down the jet's hadronic power share and top proton energies of a few PeV. The same collisions should make neutrinos, detectable by next generation telescopes. The team then simulates a whole galactic population of microquasars. About fourteen of them could explain the highest energy diffuse glow seen over the inner galaxy. Microquasar jets may be major engines of the galaxy's most energetic light.
arxiv-2512-06239:
Dhanasekar Sundararaman, Keying Li, Wayne Xiong, and Aashna Garg present LOCUS, a cheap way to build language tools for a new task from just a few examples. Their pipeline hunts through a large store of text for items close to the handful of labeled cases a user can supply. It then makes fresh training items in the same style, and tunes a model on the mix.

The tuning can be full or light weight, which keeps memory use low. On tests for finding named items in text and for sorting text into classes, LOCUS beat strong baselines, even a top commercial model, while using far fewer resources. Light tuned models kept nearly all of the accuracy of full tuning with a small share of the memory. The work targets teams that need custom language tools but lack big labeled sets and big budgets.
arxiv-2512-06339:
Taesoo Song and Jiaxing Zhao study how bound pairs of heavy quarks form inside the hot soup made in high energy nuclear collisions. That soup, quark gluon plasma, can melt such pairs apart or let fresh ones form when two heavy quarks meet. The bound states that survive, called quarkonium, act as probes of how hot and dense the soup was.

Their tool, the Remler method, projects a quark pair onto a bound state when the state can form or when one quark is scattered by the medium. Past work used it well for loosely bound states. Song and Zhao extend it to tightly bound states by adding the pull between the quark pair into the sums. With a sensible spatial cutoff, they find the pull boosts bound state formation, and results match a simpler statistical model in box tests. The work sharpens a probe of extreme matter.
arxiv-2512-06439:
Luna Rampinelli and seven co authors image water vapor glowing at the wall of a gap in the disc around a young star. The star, HD 100546, is ringed by a disc with a cleared inner cavity. Using the ALMA telescope array, the team mapped the main form of water in the disc at fine detail, a first of its kind.

The vapor peaks right where the warm dust cavity's inner wall stands, a short span from the star. The authors read this as ice turning straight to vapor where starlight hits the cavity wall head on: the water snowline, pushed outward by the bare exposure. The glow sits inside the first dust ring, matching past ALMA finds of complex organic molecules freed the same way in this disc. Warm cavities in such discs now look like prime targets for picturing water in forming planetary systems.
arxiv-2512-06639:
Zaniar Ahmadi and Frederic Godin teach a machine to hedge interest rate bets. A swaption gives its holder the right to enter an interest rate swap later, and sellers must hedge that promise as markets move. The classic hedge leans on sensitivity measures, adjusting holdings by fixed rules of thumb. Deep hedging instead lets a reinforcement learning agent learn the hedge by doing, inside a simulated market.

The authors train agents under three different goals: low average error, low downside risk, and low tail risk, each shaping a distinct hedging style. Their market model has three driving factors and no arbitrage. Two swaps as hedging tools proved nearly optimal. The learned hedges reshaped their exposure as market states changed, and they kept beating the classic hedge even when the model behind the test was somewhat wrong. The work backs learning based hedges as tougher and more efficient.
arxiv-2512-06739:
Zhichao Dong and five co authors design a way for many users to share one optical quantum link without taking turns. Coherent states of light are the workhorse of optical quantum communication. They are not fully distinct from each other. That overlap suits a multiple access scheme where users transmit at once, and a receiver peels their signals apart one by one. That pairing had not been explored for this kind of link.

The team builds such a receiver and a rule for how much power each user should send. They derive the system's total data rate in the limit of long messages, accounting for air turbulence, background noise, and photon loss. An iterative method then tunes the powers to lift that rate, with a lighter variant for many users that samples what matters most. Simulations show clear rate gains for this non orthogonal sharing over plainer designs.
arxiv-2512-06839:
Shuyuan Fan and Qi Zhang study the energy bookkeeping of particles that both drift smoothly and make sudden jumps, a model used across non-equilibrium physics. Such jump diffusions mix steady Brownian wandering with abrupt Poisson kicks, and they need not settle into the balanced state that simpler systems reach. The authors work out how free energy drains away in this general setting, with no balance assumed.

Their formula splits the drain into two parts: true entropy production, and housekeeping heat that merely keeps the system running. They also split the rule that drives the motion into a reversible half and a circulating half. The first half governs decay through a spread-out version of Fisher information. The second half produces endless circulation with no energy cost. Worked examples drawn from particle transport inside cells show how the split clarifies states that look steady yet stay restless underneath.
arxiv-2512-07039:
Antonio De Rosa and Alessandro Pigati construct surfaces of least area in settings where surface tension depends on direction. Their route runs through an equation from analysis, the direction-dependent Allen-Cahn energy, whose stable special points are known to gather along surfaces. The authors first prove a gradient bound of Modica type for those points, controlling how sharply solutions can vary. Bounds for stable answers, and for answers of bounded unsteadiness, complete the toolbox.

With those bounds, rescaled energy densities are shown to gather along a general surface that is stationary for the energy. The payoff is a min-max building: a possibly singular hypersurface obtained by sweeping the energy landscape, now in that directional world. That mirrors a celebrated isotropic result of Hutchinson and Tonegawa.
arxiv-2512-07239:
Jiro Shimoda, Katsuaki Asano, and Shu-ichiro Inutsuka follow cosmic rays as they escape their birthplaces and push on the gas between the stars. Simulations in spherical symmetry track the escaping particles, their evolving energy spectrum, the gas's radiative cooling, and heat conduction all together. Depending on how freely the cosmic rays diffuse, they accelerate and heat the interstellar gas around the source to different degrees.

That heating may explain a surprise in recent observations: glowing hydrogen and oxygen lines around old supernova remnants that should have gone quiet. The outflow the rays drive can rival the galaxy's star formation rate, strong enough to be the galactic wind that carries metals into the halo. Closer to home, assuming diffusion is locally suppressed and a few sources sit inside the Local Bubble. The authors offer fresh readings of the proton spectrum measured near Earth by several instruments.
arxiv-2512-07439:
Francisco Rodrigues wrote this 2025 review paper on the study of complex networks. Networks appear in social ties, transport, biology, and many other systems. Their records are often incomplete, rough, or gathered only by indirect means.

Rodrigues surveys recent progress on working with such flawed network data. One part covers how to sample a network and how to compare one network with another. Another part covers guessing missing links and rebuilding a network from time series data. He draws together ideas from statistics and from machine learning. He also points to open directions for sharper tools. The result is a compact map of the main methods for readers who study connected systems. It closes with his view of where the field should head next.
arxiv-2512-07539:
Qingyuan Yang, Shizhuo Deng, Dongyue Chen, Da Teng, and Zehua Gan wrote this 2025 machine learning paper. Forecasting long time series with transformers runs into a wall of cost. Their attention step grows with the square of the sequence length.

Transformers also make poor use of frequency information hidden in the data. The authors build FRWKV to attack both limits at once. Its design borrows the linear-time attention of the RWKV family of models. It then adds frequency-domain analysis to enrich the features over time. The attention path now scales in a straight line with length. Spectral detail, like cycles and rhythms, enters the model directly. On eight real-world datasets, FRWKV takes the best average rank. Removing either the linear attention or the frequency encoder hurts results. Speed and spectrum awareness, the study shows, can pull together. The code is shared in public for other teams to test.
arxiv-2512-07639:
Yulia Petrova and Nikita Rastegaev wrote this 2025 mathematics paper on conservation laws. Their system models a chemical flood, where a chemical agent changes how fluids flow. A uniqueness theorem says such a system cannot have two different valid solutions.

Kružkov-type results of that kind previously needed a tame flow function. The function had to keep an S-shape or stay monotone in the chemical level. Petrova and Rastegaev drop those restrictions almost entirely. Their theorem covers nearly arbitrary flow functions for the initial-boundary problem. They then aim the result at the classic Riemann problem. There, an S-shaped flow function flips its monotonicity exactly once. All possible solution structures for that case are classified in full. Some structures in the list have never been described before. Flood modelers gain a firmer grip on which wave patterns can occur. Uniqueness plus a complete catalog rules out phantom solutions.
arxiv-2512-07839:
Ghaura Mahabaduge wrote this 2025 mathematics paper on a geometry puzzle about dot grids. Can a polygon with all sides equal live on a planar integer lattice? For many side counts the question stayed open for particular lattice shapes.

Maehara had shown it is enough to study rectangular lattices of a special form. Those lattices stretch one axis by the square root of a whole number. The admissible numbers are those leaving a remainder of three on division by four. Building on Maehara and on Iino and Sakiyama, Mahabaduge settles the pattern. For every such lattice, some threshold side count exists. Beyond that threshold, every larger polygon count can be realized equilaterally. Short polygons may still fail, but the long run is fully covered. The result extends earlier classifications of lattice polygons.
arxiv-2512-08439:
Qing Xu, Kun Yuan, Yuxiang Luo, and colleagues, medical imaging researchers, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025. Their foundation model, LapFM, segments laparoscopic surgery video, outlining anatomy, tissue, and instruments. Surgical segmentation suffers from scarce labels and inconsistent naming across procedures, and simply fine tuning a general model makes it a narrow adapter rather than a true surgical foundation.

LapFM pre trains on masses of unlabeled surgical images through a hierarchy of concepts. A concept hierarchy ties fine labels to coarser parents, so anatomy, tissue, and instrument meanings stay consistent at every scale. A confidence driven labeling loop then generates draft labels, filters them for consistency, and folds the reliable ones back into training. That process built a benchmark of well over a hundred thousand image and mask pairs. In extensive tests, LapFM beat leading methods by a wide margin, a general base for surgical scene understanding.
arxiv-2512-08539:
Chang Qi Hu, Chun Yuan Li, Xiao Liang, Xing Hua Yang, and Dai Xing Zhang, particle theorists in China, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025. Neutrino experiments have proven that neutrinos have mass and that lepton flavors mix, but the pattern behind those masses is unexplained. Flavor symmetry is a leading tool for explaining it.

The authors propose a staged breaking scheme for a doubled permutation symmetry acting on left and right handed leptons. The symmetry first breaks to a smaller pair of subgroups, in three distinct ways, and then disappears entirely. For each route they work out the allowed forms of the mass matrices, and all three scenarios agree well with current oscillation data. Each also predicts a specific value for the CP violating phase that future experiments can test. Symmetry breaking, done in steps, can naturally produce the observed lepton pattern.
arxiv-2512-08739:
Baptiste Coquinot and coauthors show that a supersolid can form at the boundary between a superfluid and a solid, without changing the bulk interactions. A supersolid combines superfluid flow with crystal order, and had mainly been made by tuning forces inside a cold gas. Here the driver is coupling between modes at the interface itself.

Using analytic and numerical treatment of the coupled superfluid and phonon fields, the team derives when a density modulation becomes unstable. In superfluid helium the effect starts at the roton mode, while in a contact interacting condensate it starts at the lowest wave allowed by system size. Past the threshold, the interface gains a pattern while the bulk stays superfluid. The result suggests a broad route to hybrid phases that use both interface and bulk quantum traits.
arxiv-2512-08839:
Katherine Atwell, Saki Imai, Danielle Bragg, and Malihe Alikhani report a global survey of Deaf and hard of hearing community members on sign language technologies. Interest in such tools is growing in industry and research, yet community views are often sidelined, especially outside the West and in the global South. The survey spans many countries, sign languages, and cultural contexts.

Participants saw promise in the tools for access and independence, but many raised concerns. Worries included cultural erasure, inaccurate translation, and research pipelines led mainly by hearing people. Views were shaped by sign language skill, policy exposure, and deaf identity. Across regions, participants stressed Deaf led design and warned of harm when communities are excluded from decisions. The authors close with concrete recommendations for researchers, technologists, and policymakers who build or fund sign language technology.
arxiv-2512-09039:
Mandev Bhullar, Philip Richard, and Hae Young Kee study a pseudospin chain with competing couplings. The one dimensional transverse Ising model is a classic example of quantum criticality. In spin orbit coupled systems, extra Kitaev and Gamma terms join the usual Heisenberg exchange,.

The authors explore a generic model with four fold screw symmetry and track how sublattice order appears. Below the critical field, the order depends on the sublattice, and a distinct sublattice pattern persists above the field as well. Despite that complex structure, the field driven transition stays in the Ising universality class, with the expected central charge. The work gives a route to the microscopic Hamiltonian behind the criticality, while letting sublattice physics show at both low and high fields. A known antiferromagnetic Ising material is discussed as an application of the theory.
arxiv-2512-09239:
Juan Diego Belesaca and Fabian Astudillo Salinas set out a plan, called a protocol, for a systematic review of ways to measure water flow in pipes without cutting into them. Accurate flow measurement matters for managing water supplies and spotting leaks. Many external sensing tools now exist, but their performance has not been pulled together in one place.

Following the Kitchenham method for systematic reviews, the planned study will collect and compare published evidence on techniques such as ultrasonic sensors and vibration sensors attached outside the pipe. It will weigh accuracy, precision, and energy use, and ask how signal processing and machine learning improve the readings. The protocol's goal is to map what is known, expose the gaps, and give future work a solid base for moving these tools into real water networks.
arxiv-2512-09639:
Leonardo L. Bosnardo and Marcus A. M. de Aguiar study how to simplify networks of synchronized oscillators by treating modules as units. Many networks are modular, with tight communities inside them, and dynamics like synchronization depend on that structure. Their inspiration is electroencephalography, where each electrode averages groups of neurons into one node of a correlation network.

For Kuramoto oscillators, the model of synchronization, placed on modular networks, they propose a coarse-graining procedure that replaces each well-synchronized module with one oscillator. They map out how the coupling strengths inside and between modules decide whether the reduction stays meaningful. For networks with two and three modules, the reduced systems describe the transition from disorder to synchrony well regardless of how the modules are wired together. Tests on networks show the approximation holds when each module's oscillators are identical, even reproducing patterns for modules that synchronize poorly on their own.
arxiv-2512-09739:
Bartosz Zbik and colleagues solve a timing problem with a twist: how long does it take a wandering stochastic process to first reach a target that keeps blinking on and off? First hitting times matter across biology, chemistry, and economics. Here the target switches between active and inactive states, and only hits registered while the target is active count.

The authors derive closed formulas for the distribution of the first hitting time in this blinking setup. They then add stochastic resetting, where the process is repeatedly returned to its start, and adapt their results to get the first active hit under resetting. A subtlety emerges: resetting in this setup leaves the system with memory, breaking the Markov property that standard techniques rely on, which the analysis must work around. The analytical results are accompanied by computer simulations of Langevin dynamics, the model of a particle buffeted by random noise.
arxiv-2512-09939:
Stella C. Dong models reinsurance decisions as a game among rule bound agents. Reinsurance resists simple automation: facts are uneven, models drive outcomes, and solvency rules bind every choice. Dong proposes a formal model, the Reinsurance Constrained Multi-Agent Simulation Process, which extends stochastic games and decentralized decision models with three added parts.

The parts are simulator coupled dynamics, role specialized agents with structured beliefs and typed messages, and a rules layer that turns prudential rules into constraints on which joint actions are allowed. In a test world tuned to the domain, language model agents with tools followed this design. Governed coordination proved more stable and rule abiding than set automation or one big single model. Pricing variance fell, capital use improved, and clause readings grew more exact.
arxiv-2512-10039:
Jack Arce and Cristian Vay attack a classification problem in Hopf algebra theory. The objects are liftings: deformations of a construction called the bosonization of a Nichols algebra over a Hopf algebra. The hard cases are non semisimple, arising when the field has positive characteristic or the algebra is infinite dimensional. The authors introduce a generalized algebra built from an extension module. It reduces to the usual bosonization when the extension is trivial. They give necessary conditions for it to be a Hopf algebra.

Their main theorem says every lifting is a quotient of one of these generalized algebras. From that fulcrum, an existing strategy can be adapted to show every lifting is a cocycle deformation. They classify all pointed liftings of the Fomin-Kirillov algebra in characteristic two, and treat a Jordanian enveloping algebra example.
arxiv-2512-10339:
Ziseok Lee and co-authors study steering, a way to adapt trained diffusion and flow models to new tasks at run time without retraining. Steering often blends several expert models by reweighting their densities. But the authors name a failure, marginal path collapse, where the blended intermediate density stops being a valid distribution even though the endpoints are fine.

Collapse tends to strike when experts were trained with mismatched noise schedules or partial support. The paper gives a sharp path existence criterion that tells when the composed densities are well defined, plus a correction method that lets the blending weights vary over time. On a drug design task mixing three experts, the correction prevented collapse and beat fixed-weight baselines, and it also improved success rates in compositional image generation.
arxiv-2512-10939:
Madhav Agarwal and co-authors make talking heads that do not wobble. Speech-driven avatars are ready for interactive use only if they are fast, faithful, and stable. And current methods split that triangle: diffusion models look real but are slow and weak in one-shot settings. While Gaussian splatting runs in real time but inherits jitter from faulty face tracking and inconsistent Gaussian placement.

GaussianHeadTalk anchors its Gaussians to a 3D morphable model of the face, so the avatar is person-specific and the splats stay registered. A transformer predicts the model's parameters directly from the audio, which keeps motion temporally consistent instead of frame-by-frame shaky. Given a monocular video of the person plus separate speech audio, the system generates real-time talking-head video. The authors report competitive quantitative and qualitative results at the Winter Conference on Applications of Computer Vision 2026.
arxiv-2512-11039:
Benjamin Stölzner and colleagues use the final Kilo-Degree Survey data to test Horndeski gravity, a broad family of theories that modify Einstein's gravity with an extra scalar field. They combine weak lensing measurements with galaxy clustering, distance markers, and cosmic microwave background data. Their analysis uses a formulation designed so that stability is guaranteed from the start.

Weak lensing alone constrained the modified gravity parameters about as strongly as the microwave background did. Some measures of how gravity differs from Einstein's value sat a few standard deviations away, and modified gravity fit the data slightly better. A formal model comparison, however, found only weak preference for the modified theory. The inferred amount of cosmic structure stayed close to the standard model value, and results held steady when the background cosmology was allowed evolving dark energy.
arxiv-2512-11139:
Tathagata Sadhukhan and colleagues speed up a core choice in Lasso regression, the popular method that selects a sparse set of predictors from many candidates. Lasso needs a tuning parameter, normally chosen by cross validation. That search is slow and loses accuracy when data are high dimensional and noisy, and it gets worse for time series models.

Their strategy, called autotune, lets a single Lasso fit tune itself. Quantities computed during the fit, called partial residuals, reveal both the noise level and which predictors matter, and alternating between those estimates settles on a good parameter value. Tests on regression and time series models show faster and more accurate tuning than existing options, especially at low signal strength. The method also estimates noise levels and produces diagnostic plots, and an R package is available.
arxiv-2512-11539:
Néstor Armesto and fellow authors model how the exotic particle X(3872) would be produced in heavy ion collisions if it is a compact four quark state. The particle's internal structure remains unsettled, and collisions that recreate quark gluon plasma offer a discriminating test. Free heavy quarks in the plasma can recombine into bound states as it cools.

The team derives a coalescence model from the Lindblad equation, which governs open quantum systems, assuming the unbound quarks are thermalised and an adiabatic approximation holds. Proton proton data supply the baseline. Their prediction is a clear yield enhancement in heavy ion collisions, because recombination dominates production for a tetraquark. The resulting nuclear modification factor, comparing collision yields with the scaled baseline, becomes a powerful observable for probing what this unusual state really is.
arxiv-2601-06739:
Daniel Munoz George and co-authors study random monomial ideals from large graphs in 2026. Their model is inspired by the Erdos-Renyi model of random graphs. They propose a new model for squarefree random monomial ideals.

The ideals are generated by edges and covers of a graph, they explain. This permits investigating conditions of normality for such random ideals. For those conditions they obtain asymptotic results in the paper. As graphs grow large, probabilities settle into patterns they compute. Random ideals connect combinatorics, probability, and commutative algebra in one object. Their edge-and-cover generation ties ideal theory tightly to graph structure. Algebraists get limit theorems for when random ideals stay normal. The work extends random graph thinking into polynomial ring territory.
arxiv-2601-06939:
David D. Dai and co-authors published a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint covers essentially no energy barrier between independent fermionic neural quantum state minima. It appeared in the arXiv PAPERS collection for 2026. Neural quantum states (NQS) have proven highly effective in representing quantum many-body wavefunctions, but their loss landscape remains poorly understood and debated.

Here, we show that the NQS loss landscape is more benign and similar to conventional deep learning than previously thought. Exhibiting mode connectivity: independently trained NQS are connected by paths in parameter space with essentially no energy barrier. The preprint gives researchers a focused account of the problem and the approach the authors take.
arxiv-2601-07039:
Lihong Guo, Harry Ip, and Mingyang Wang wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on a swinging system with a lag in its spring. The system is a bilinear oscillator, driven by white noise. Such a model sees wide use in design and build work. It can show strong bends in how a metal acts, such as the Bauschinger effect.

Most teams find the long-run spread of the swing by Monte Carlo runs, which test the model with random draws again and again. The authors take a new path based on a PDE, an equation for how a spread shifts over time. Their path builds on the elasto-plastic frame set out by Bensoussan and co-authors. For a reader in this field, the paper gives a direct way to get the long-run spread. It skips the cost of vast numbers of random runs.
arxiv-2601-07139:
Junhong Zou and co-authors published a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint covers AdaField. It appeared in the arXiv PAPERS collection for 2026. The surface pressure field of transportation systems, including cars, trains, and aircraft, is critical for aerodynamic analysis and design. In recent years, deep neural networks have emerged as promising and efficient methods for modeling surface pressure field.

Being alternatives to computationally expensive CFD simulations. Currently, large-scale public datasets are available for domains such as automotive aerodynamics. The preprint gives researchers a focused account of the problem and the approach the authors take.
arxiv-2601-07339: Victoria Motsch and co-authors published a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint covers impact of boundary conditions on the Double-Kicked quantum rotor. It appeared in the arXiv PAPERS collection for 2026. The authors study the on-resonance Spin-1/2 Double Kicked Rotor, a periodically driven quantum system that hosts topological phases. Motivated by experimental constraints, the authors analyze the effects of open and periodic boundary conditions. In contrast to the idealized case of infinite momentum space. The preprint gives researchers a focused account of the problem and the approach the authors take.
arxiv-2601-07439:
Julián Garrido and co-authors posted a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint deals with advanced computing for reproducibility of astronomy big data science, with a showcase. It came out on arXiv in 2026 as a PAPERS preprint. The Square Kilometre Array Observatory (SKAO) faces unprecedented technological challenges due to the vast scale and complexity of its data. The work provides an overview of research by the AMIGA group to address these computing and reproducibility challenges.

The authors present advancements in semantic data models. Analysis services integrated into federated infrastructures, and the application to astronomy studies of techniques that enhance research transparency. Readers in the field get a short, focused account of the problem and the steps the authors take.
arxiv-2601-07539:
Ryo Okano and Daisuke Kurisu extend a popular causal method to outcomes that live in abstract spaces. The synthetic control method estimates the effect of a policy by building a weighted copy of the treated unit. Recent work lets outcomes be distributions, functions, networks, or covariance matrices rather than single numbers. Their 2026 preprint develops functional synthetic control methods for such metric space-valued outcomes.

When outcomes are curves or distributions, ordinary averaging and fitting need rethinking. Functional versions must respect the geometry of the outcome space. Sound methods here matter for policy studies where the outcome is a whole distribution, like income or health profiles. The paper speaks to econometricians and statisticians evaluating interventions with complex outcomes. It aims to give the method a firmer theoretical base.
arxiv-2601-07639:
Norm Levenberg and Sione Ma'u develop potential theory on algebraic curves, in a 2026 mathematics preprint. Earlier work by the second author defined directional Robin constants for a compact, nonpolar subset of a curve. The curve sits inside complex space of several dimensions. Robin constants measure how a set interacts with growth of analytic functions. The authors relate these constants to a natural class of Chebyshev constants for the same set.

Chebyshev constants govern best polynomial approximation on a set. Linking two kinds of constants lets results pass between potential theory and approximation theory. Algebraic curves give the theory concrete, structured sets to work on. The paper is aimed at specialists in pluripotential theory and complex analysis. It continues a line of work the authors have built over several papers.
arxiv-2601-07839:
Pawan Kumar and Aditi Gupta compress large language models with a two-stage scheme that respects their weight structure. Modern LLMs strain memory and compute budgets, for both deployment and further training. Their method, Hierarchical Sparse Plus Low-Rank compression, first removes the largest-magnitude weights into a sparse matrix. It then factorizes the remaining dense matrix with a recursive hierarchical low-rank method. The work appears as a 2026 preprint.

Splitting weights this way keeps the few big weights exact while compressing the many small ones. Hierarchical factorization exploits structure at several scales. Principled compression decides whether a model can run on available hardware at all. The paper speaks to machine learning engineers facing deployment limits. It offers compression as a designed procedure, not a blunt cut.
arxiv-2601-07939:
Shireesh Reddy Pyreddy and colleagues present SECite, a tool that reads how later papers treat an earlier one. Judging a paper's strengths and limits is core to any literature review. Standard summaries only reflect the authors' own view of their work. Citations reveal how the community actually used, praised, or criticized it. Their 2026 preprint builds analysis and summarization around those citations in software engineering literature.

A citation can signal endorsement, routine use, or disagreement. Telling these apart gives a deeper, more practical picture of a paper. SECite aims to summarize that reception automatically. Scholars drowning in reading lists could triage papers faster. The tool also exposes limitations that authors would not advertise. The paper serves software engineering scholars and tool builders. It treats citations as evidence, not just counts.
arxiv-2601-08539: Jeffrey Spaan, Kuan-Hsun Chen, and Ana-Lucia Varbanescu cut compute waste in language models with kernel-level frequency scaling. Their 2026 arXiv paper notes that AI growth has expanded GPU data centers fast. Rising operational energy use has become a critical bottleneck and sustainability concern. Dynamic voltage and frequency scaling lowers energy use with existing hardware and little effort. Applying it at kernel level targets the moments when full GPU speed is wasted. Such tuning could trim data center bills without slowing model serving.
arxiv-2601-08639:
Six authors, led by Tanmay Inamdar, study a hard choice problem on graphs. A graph here is a set of points joined by lines. The task is to pick a small set of red points that cover many blue points. The picked set must also stay joined as one piece. Past work treats each part of this task on its own.

The team gives one shared model for the whole task. They then look for fast methods that get close to the best pick. The methods run in time that stays fixed for a key size in the task. Such work helps when a network must serve many users but can build links at only a few hubs. A reader gets both the model and the near best methods.
arxiv-2601-08739:
Xingyu Tan and six co-authors work on safe use of fact graphs by chat models. A fact graph stores facts as linked triples, such as a name, a link, and a value. Such graphs can ground a model and cut made up claims. But many graphs hold private facts that must not leak to a closed model host.

Their tool is called PrivGemo. It uses two towers, one on the user side and one for search. The private graph stays on the safe side while the model still gets the facts it needs. No raw triples need to cross to the host. A reader who must guard data gets a plan for strong search with less leak risk.
arxiv-2601-08839:
Toshiyuki Shigemura builds a team of three chat models that check each other in a loop. One model drafts text. A next model checks if the draft holds up. A third model checks if the work is clear and can be traced. The loop runs more than once, so each round can fix the last.

He calls this loop Recursive Knowledge Synthesis. The claim is that the loop makes a whole that no one model can match on its own. He also gives ways to test if the loop stays stable, or if it drifts with each round. A reader who builds model teams gets both a plan and a test frame. It helps judge when a team loop helps, and when it just adds cost.
arxiv-2601-08939:
B. Moreschini and a large team warn that one cloud form can skew chem counts in far galaxies. The Webb scope lets us read the gas in such galaxies with tools honed nearby. Near tools rest on calm gas states. Far gas is far more wild, with strong light and low metal counts. A calm form may not fit it at all.

The team shows how wild states shift the lines we read. If we force a one cloud form, the chem counts we get can be off by much. More than one cloud state must be let in the fit. A reader who reads far gas gets a clear warn. Old near tools need a fresh check at high range.
arxiv-2601-09239:
Hanlin Zhang and eight co-authors split speech into two code streams: sense and sound. A speech code turns a wave into a short list of codes a chat model can use. Past codes mix what was said with how it sounds. That mix makes it hard to swap voice yet keep words, or to keep voice and change words.

Their code tool is called DSA-Tokenizer. It holds sense codes and sound codes apart by set rules in train. A flow match step then joins the two in a ranked way for the next stage. A reader in speech tech gets a split code that may serve voice swap and text true tasks at once.
arxiv-2601-09539:
Nataniel Marquis works on deep conjectures that link two sides of the p-adic Langlands program. His 2026 arXiv paper weighs what conjectures by Breuil, Herzig, Hu, Morra, and Schraen imply for Zábrádi's functor. On one side sit representations of the p-adic Galois group; on the other, representations of GL_n over the p-adic numbers. When a Galois representation is generic and well placed, a notion of compatibility ties the two sides. Papers like this one test whether the grand conjectures of the field fit together without clashes.

The paper is a work of pure mathematics. It sits in the p-adic Langlands program, a long effort to link Galois groups with linear groups.
arxiv-2601-09639:
Y. Kilic and a large team pin down the size and shape of Ixion, a large world beyond Neptune. Their 2026 arXiv paper uses multi-chord stellar occultations of the trans-Neptunian object (28978) Ixion. When such a body crosses a star, its shadow gives a sharp outline.

Trans-Neptunian objects are among the most primitive leftovers of the early solar system. Occultations give accurate sizes and shapes, while photometry constrains albedo and surface colors. Several chords across the shadow trace Ixion's true outline. Knowing one large body's form in detail anchors models of how the outer system was built.
arxiv-2601-10039:
C. R. Skolar and B. Srinivasan study the thin layer that forms near a wall in a plasma. The work is set in a Z-pinch, a fusion test bed. In such a bed, plasma is held in a tube. A bias is set on the end plates.

The field lines run along the wall, not across it. That case has had few past tests. The pair run a full sim of a cut through the pinch. They solve for the grains and the field as one. The sim shows how the layer forms when hits are rife and the field runs flat to the wall.
arxiv-2601-10339:
Xue-Nan Chen tests if gravity can tell quantum stuffs apart. The weak equivalence rule says all stuff falls the same. Its quantum form is still an open ask. In quantum work, chance is part of each claim. A test must code that chance in full.

Chen sets the rule in terms of a scatter spread. At tree level, that spread is worked out for a light grain off a heavy one. The claim is that the spread does not rest on the grain's mass or kind. The heavy mass cap makes the test sharp. The work gives a form for the quantum rule.
arxiv-2601-10639:
Ranajoy Sadhukhan and co-authors present STEM, a way to scale transformer models with less compute per token. Sparse designs promise more capacity without a matching rise in cost. In practice they often suffer unstable training, poor load balance, and heavy traffic between chips. STEM takes a static, token-indexed route instead.

The method swaps the up-projection in each feed-forward block for a lookup in a local embedding table. The gate and down-projection stay dense, as before. Lookups are cheap, so capacity can grow while token cost stays low. The design targets teams that train large language models and want size without runaway bills.
arxiv-2601-10939:
Christopher J. Butler and co-authors report liquid-crystal-like electronic order living alongside superconductivity in NaAlSi. Electronic nematic and smectic phases break symmetry in the electron fluid itself. They often appear near or inside unconventional superconducting states. NaAlSi is a semimetal with a silicon square net, and its superconductivity is thought to be unconventional.

Using scanning tunneling microscopy, the team observed short-range charge stripe order, the smectic pattern. The stripes coexist with superconductivity in the same material. That coexistence is a clue about how the two orders relate: rivals, partners, or two faces of one cause. The work adds a clean case to the study of quantum materials.
arxiv-2601-11339:
Shangjie Tian and nine coauthors name a new topological insulator in this work. Their 2026 preprint studies the compound Ge2Bi2Te5 in layered form. Topological insulators pass current on their surface only. Their bulk stays inert, which makes them rare and prized.

Most known cases are binary compounds of two elements. The search has moved to ternary mixes for new physics. This compound joins germanium, bismuth, and tellurium in one stack. The team identifies it as a 3D topological insulator. New members of this class feed both physics and devices. They may host exotic states that future chips can use.
arxiv-2601-11539:
Dinanath Padhya and four coauthors build a low-cost sensor glove for sign language. Their 2026 preprint reports the design and implementation in full. Severe hearing loss affects over 430 million people worldwide. Access to sign language interpretation stays critically scarce.

The gap bites hardest in low-resource settings like Nepal. Assistive tools split into two flawed camps today. Commercial gloves often cost more than 3,000 dollars. Research gloves use flex sensors that degrade fast under stress. The team's glove uses Hall-effect sensors instead of flex ones. Hall sensors read magnetic fields as fingers move. The aim is a cheap, tough glove that lasts.
arxiv-2601-11739:
Xinyu Pi, Qisen Yang, Chuong Nguyen, and Hua Shen map how large language models are now used in work with words and themes. Such work, called qualitative analysis, reads texts to find sense and themes. Model output can range from plain sums of what was said to full models of a system.

To make these gaps clear, they build a grid with four rows and four cols. One axis lists four levels of sense making, from plain facts to full theory. The other lists four levels of form, from fixed maps to loops that feed back. The grid helps teams state what a tool does and does not do.
arxiv-2601-12939:
