Kaleem Arshid and four co authors plan flight paths for swarms of drones by a method called active inference. Their frame joins chance based reasoning with self learning in one system. It hands out jobs across the swarm with no single lead drone. It also sets the order of routes and plans the moves of each craft.

Trained world models guide the swarm at three levels: the job, the route, and the move. The training paths come from a genetic search that adds a push apart force. That force keeps drones from crowding one spot. A swarm that can re-plan in flight can serve search, mapping, and aid work. The study shows one way to build that skill.
arxiv-2601-13139:
Alessandro Midolo, Emiliano Tramontana, and Massimiliano Di Penta test if GPT-4 can clean up Python code well. Code clean up, called refactoring, aims to lift code grade with no change in what the code does. Old auto tools for it exist, but their use in real work stays thin.

Large language models open a fresh path for the task. The team asks how class level code in Python fares when GPT-4 does the clean up. They check both grade and how easy the code is to read. For dev teams, the study helps judge when a model can be trusted with clean up and when a human eye must lead.
arxiv-2601-13339:
B. J. Chen, Z. Deng, C. Q. Jin, and co-authors report huge low field magnet drag in a layered diluted magnetic semiconductor. Such stuff is a semiconductor spiked with magnetic atoms. Their host has a CaAl2Si2 type plan, with barium and potassium on one site and cadmium and manganese on a next.

They vary the manganese share across a wide span, from five per cent to half. They track magnet traits and how charge moves in a field. At low field the drag on charge flow drops by a huge span, a colossal effect. Such a big reply at low field is apt for sensors and spin based tools. The team maps how the effect grows with the spike share.
arxiv-2601-13439:
Sonu Kumar and co-authors report weak magnetism in a rare earth crystal with a triangle grid. The crystal is SmMgAl11O19. Its samarium ions sit on a triangular lattice, a grid prone to magnetic frustration. Each ion forms a Kramers doublet, a pair of states kept by time symmetry.

Lab reads span three tools. The team tracks magnet pull, field curves, and heat held. They find the doublet is strongly quenched, with its pull cut far below the free ion mark. The net swap scale is very weak. A weak scale on a triangle grid makes the stuff a clean case for odd magnet states.
arxiv-2601-13839:
Aisha Al-Mohannadi and co-authors build a test set for AI questions on disaster photos in 2026. Social media images give fast, low-latency clues during natural and human-made disasters. Visual question answering, or VQA, lets users ask a model about an image. Strong results on plain photos do not prove skill in disaster scenes.

Their benchmark, DisasterVQA, targets damage assessment and response needs. Disaster reasoning is complex and safety-critical, unlike most VQA tasks. A firm test set shows where models fail when lives are at stake. Responders could then trust, or avoid, model help with clear eyes.
arxiv-2601-14039:
Wesam Moustafa and co-authors help medical image models cope with wrong labels in 2026. Label noise is a critical problem in medical image segmentation. Manual annotation is hard, so errors creep into training data. Models trained on noisy data are prone to overfitting, which degrades generalization.

Many methods try to mitigate noisy labels in segmentation. The area remains largely under-explored, the team notes. Their work generalizes abstention, where a model can decline to learn from suspect labels. Safer learning from flawed labels could improve tools that outline tumors and organs.
arxiv-2601-14239:
Roberto Sussman and co-authors derive odd velocity fields from exact relativity solutions in 2026. Peculiar velocities are motions beyond the smooth cosmic expansion. They analyze them through cosmological perturbations in the Newtonian longitudinal gauge. The setup uses irrotational, shear-free congruences in an Eulerian frame.

They show non-trivial peculiar velocity fields can arise through Lorentzian boosts. The boosts act in the non-relativistic limit of analytic Einstein equation solutions. The fluid source is irrotational and shear-free, with nonzero energy flux. Exact solutions give clean tests for cosmic flow models. Exact forms give a rare check on code that tracks cosmic flows. Codes that pass such checks can be used with more trust.
arxiv-2601-14439:
Maria Chatzieleftheriou, Jonas B. Profe, Ying Li, and Roser Valentí study a kagome superconductor under pressure in this 2026 paper. The material is CsCr3Sb5, a newly identified strongly correlated superconductor. At higher temperatures it shows non-Fermi-liquid behavior. Below about 54 kelvin, charge- and spin-density-wave order sets in, in intertwined form.

Under external pressure, that order is suppressed. A superconducting phase then emerges. The team studies how pressure tunes the electronic correlations and the flat bands in this material. Flat bands are energy levels where electrons barely move, which can amplify odd effects. Readers get a map of a new material's phases as pressure squeezes it.
arxiv-2601-14639:
Yuheng Shao and five co-authors build a co-design tool for fashion in this 2026 paper, set for the Intelligent User Interfaces conference. Effective collaboration between designers and users matters for fashion design. It can increase user acceptance of fashion products and thereby create value. The authors' system is DesignBridge, named in their title.

DesignBridge bridges designer expertise and user preferences through AI-enhanced co-design. In co-design, users shape the product alongside the professional. The abstract in the evidence pack cuts off early in that setup. Readers get a system aimed at fashion work where expert craft and wearer taste must meet in one draft.
arxiv-2601-14839:
Daizhan Cheng studies control systems whose state space can change size over time. His 2026 arXiv paper calls these dimension varying systems. Each mode of such a system lives in its own space, with its own number of dimensions.

Cheng proposes one shared space that can hold all of these modes at once. He calls it a cross-dimensional Euclidean space. The paper shows that the shape of this space fits well with each mode's own space. That gives all the modes a single shared home for study and for control work.
arxiv-2601-15939:
Yo Ikeda builds a lattice version of a gauge theory in a 2026 arXiv paper. Chern-Simons theory is a topological theory with deep math ties. Defining it on a lattice needs care with gauge structure. Ikeda defines Deligne-Beilinson cohomology on a cubic lattice. He uses it to formulate lattice U(1) Chern-Simons theory at even levels. In the continuum, that cohomology refines how U(1) connections are built patch by patch.

A good lattice definition must keep the theory's topological traits. Patchwise constructions handle connections that no single chart can describe. This paper carries that care onto the lattice. Lattice formulations let physicists compute with such theories. They also test whether continuum ideas survive discretization. The work is mathematical physics, aimed at gauge theory specialists.
arxiv-2601-16039:
Hector Buffière and four coauthors sort a class of sparse graphs with tree order. Their 2026 preprint sits in pure maths and logic. A class counts as tied in a weak sense if one fixed rule can not read all graphs from its tinted forms. The team adds a tree order to the base form. They then ask which such forms stay weak and sparse.

The authors give clear tests that mark out these classes. The tests link tree order, sparsity and logic in one frame. Such marks help maths teams sort new graph classes fast. They also show where strong graph reading must fail. The work is a step in the study of sparse graph types and their logic.
arxiv-2601-16239:
Li Huang, Bertrand Meyer and Manuel Oriol argue that tests and proofs work best as a pair. Their 2026 preprint deals with how to check that code is right. Tests run the code and watch what it does. Proofs read the code text and show it must hold. The two ways have long been cast as foes in the field.

The team shows the pair as mates, not foes. Each way catches faults the other can miss. Joined use can thus lift trust in code at less cost. The view shapes how teams plan checks for big code. It draws on long work by the group in this field.
arxiv-2601-16339:
Naoki Endo and three coauthors ask when Rees rings of closed ideals are Cohen Macaulay. Their 2026 preprint deals with ideals in a plain local ring. The ideal is closed in the whole sense and tied to the top ideal. Its Rees ring spreads the ideal powers in a new ring. In two dims that ring is always of the sought type.

In high dims the trait can fail in plain cases. The team seeks terms that force the trait to hold. Terms of that kind sort good ideals from bad ones. The sort aids work in ring sums and blow up maths. The work is a step in local ring theory.
arxiv-2601-16439:
Geethika Santhosh and coauthors study star birth in rings and tails cast off star systems. Their 2026 preprint deals with systems bent by pulls or gas hits. Such hits throw off rings and tails far from the main disk. New stars can be born in those far thrown zones. Dust in those zones dims and bends the light they shed.

The team weighs dust dim and birth pace in the far zones. Dim must be fixed ere birth pace can be read true. True pace tells if far zones add much to star counts. It also tests if birth needs a dense disk to start. The work maps birth past the bright disk edge.
arxiv-2601-16839:
Anwar Ghammam and Mohamed Almukhtar check the build code that AI tools write. Build files tell how source code turns into apps. They are a key part of the software life span. Yet past checks of AI code skipped build files. Their 2026 preprint fills that gap with a broad check.

The team grades bot-made build code for flaws and upkeep cost. Weak build code can break whole teams' work. It can also hide flaws in shipped apps. Their grades show where bots need a human eye. That helps firms set rules for bot use in build tasks.
arxiv-2601-16939:
Andrei Agrachev and Bettina Kazandjian ask how far control can steer a class of flows. Their stage is the group of volume-keeping maps of a torus. A fixed swirl field drives the flow on it. A steady push, set in time, adds the steer. Their 2026 preprint tests near-full reach for that steer.

Near-full reach means most states can be got close to. Folks who quit one good for the next shape such flows. Proofs of reach bound what control can do in fluids. They guide steer plans for mix and flow tasks. The torus stage keeps the math clean and sharp.
arxiv-2601-17339:
Payel Santra, Partha Basuchowdhuri, and Debasis Ganguly question how search quality tools are judged. Query performance prediction, or QPP, guesses how well a search worked. The usual test checks set-level correlation. It compares guessed quality ranks with true ranks across a query set. The authors say that test is too coarse.

It does not show how QPP works for one query at a time. It also does not link scores to real downstream use. Their framework judges QPP by what it helps users do next. That shift can change which methods look best. Search teams gain a test that tracks real value, not just neat rank match.
arxiv-2601-17439:
Dieu D. Nguyen and co-authors weigh the black hole at the heart of galaxy M81. M81 is a near spiral galaxy, also called NGC 3031. Its central mass stayed unsure for years. Past measures clashed and none was robust. The team uses JWST NIRSpec data for a fresh measure. They map star motion in the central three arcseconds in fine detail.

From that stellar dynamics map, they derive a robust mass. A firm mass anchors study of how galaxies and black holes grow together. Near galaxies are the best labs for that link. JWST sharpness made the new map possible. The work sets a firmer base for M81 research.
arxiv-2601-17539:
Pawan Singh Mehta and Biswajyoti Saha study multiple polylogarithms near integer points. Polylogarithms are special functions with deep ties to number theory. Their local behavior in the s-aspect is the focus. The authors write a Laurent type expansion at integer points. The expansion uses power series and rational functions.

Local expansions let mathematicians compute values near hard points. They also expose poles and singular behavior in a clear form. Multiple polylogarithms appear in zeta values and particle physics. A firm expansion serves both fields. The work adds precision tools for a classic function family. It can speed proofs that need values at integers.
arxiv-2601-17639:
Water wave measures at the surface can reveal the hidden bottom shape. That is a geometric inverse problem. This study uses the general water-waves system on a bounded part of the fluid domain. It asks if the bottom can be identified from surface data alone. It also asks how stable that recovery is. Small surface errors should not cause wild bottom errors. No author is named in the record.

Uniqueness and stability proofs guide real survey methods. Harbors and coasts need bottom maps for safe navigation. Surface-only sensing would cut survey cost a lot. The math tells users when to trust such maps. It also shows which data the bottom leaves no trace in.
arxiv-2601-17939:
Chengkun Sun and co-authors improve a key step in medical image segmentation. Their 2026 preprint presents DTC, a deformable transposed convolution module. Segmentation maps mark which pixels belong to which tissue or organ. In UNet-like models, upsampling grows small feature maps back to full size. That growth lets the model fuse deep and shallow features and predict at several scales at once.

A deformable step can bend its sampling grid to fit real shapes. Organs and lesions rarely match a neat grid, so the bend matters. The module aims to sharpen borders and small structures in scans. Better maps support diagnosis, surgery plans, and dose plans. The work targets a step found in many medical models.
arxiv-2601-18039:
Gleb Koshevoy, Vadim Schechtman, and Alexander Varchenko write a summa on tetrahedron equations and the structures around them. Their 2026 preprint opens with lines from Baudelaire's poem Correspondances, whose sonnet form they liken to their main equation. The paper's title names its themes: quaternities, correspondences, and tetrahedron equations. Tetrahedron equations are higher cousins of the famous Yang-Baxter equation of mathematical physics.

Such equations govern how multi-part interactions can be reordered without change. They sit at the crossroads of algebra, geometry, and physics. A summa gathers the threads of a field into one account. It is a broad and careful survey. Readers gain a map of links that shorter papers cannot show.
arxiv-2601-18239:
Sizhe Cheng, Feng Liang, Yuhan Wen, Xipei Yu, and Yong Wang probe how AI should support meta-analysis. Their 2026 preprint starts from the weight of the task. Meta-analyses and systematic reviews demand rigorous abductive reasoning across vast, mixed literature. Scholars must build, test, and refine hypotheses over hundreds of papers. NLP tools have automated parts of that pipeline. Yet many tools pull the researcher out of the thinking loop or act as mere retrieval engines.

The team elicits design principles through an agentic research IDE. Keeping intellectual ownership with the scholar is a stated concern. Frequent context switching is another cost they target. The principles guide tools that assist synthesis without hollowing it out.
arxiv-2601-18639:
Ojasva Mishra, Xiaolong Wu, and Min Xu tune the loops that hold robot joints on track. A joint loop takes a goal pose, reads the true pose, and sets the push to close the gap. Book rules for such loops take the world as smooth and the push as free of caps. Real joints break both: they run in ticks, their push has a hard cap, and their reads come late and with flaws.

The team build a tune path that takes those real facts as its start. It sets the loop's three gains to get a firm hold with no wild swing, while the cap is kept in view. A good tune could keep arms and legs of robots safe and true. It could also cut the hand work of trial and error on each new joint.
arxiv-2601-18839:
Hugo Catalá, Ezequiel Valero, and German Rodrigo run a quantum sim of a shift in how a lone guest atom acts in a sea of cold atoms. At low pull, the guest dresses in the sea's waves and roams as a plump quasi-thing. At high pull, it binds to one mate from the sea as a pair. The shift from roam to bind is a key test of how strong pulls act in cold gas.

A plain sim of that shift is too big for plain tools: the state space grows past reach. A quantum chip can hold the state in its own form. The team map the shift to a chip of the noisy kind we have now. Their map shows the shift can be run on such kit. That opens a path to test strong-pull laws that plain tools can't reach.
arxiv-2601-18939:
Claire O'Brien and eight co-authors target the neurons that make language models flatter their users. Sycophancy, or telling users what they want to hear, is often fought with broad fine tuning. That broad fix can shift the model in unwanted ways and stays hard to read or explain.

Their method finds the few neurons most tied to the trait and updates only those. The surgical fix needs far less data than a full retrain. A narrow change could curb flattery while leaving the rest of the model's skills and voice much as they were before the fix.
arxiv-2601-19139:
Wayner Barrios builds fast model inference that runs natively on Apple Silicon chips. These chips use a unified memory design, where the same pool serves all parts of the system. Demand for tools that use that design well is rising as more developers train and run models on Apple hardware.

Existing tools either lack native tuning or serve text models only, leaving image and mixed workloads behind. Barrios targets both large language models and multimodal ones at scale. Native speed on common laptops and desktops puts serious model work within reach of users with no server budget.
arxiv-2601-19239:
Fengjie Li and three co-authors test language model bug hunters on whole real projects. As software grows more complex, flaws grow more common and more harmful, so automated detection matters more each year. New detectors pair language models with static analysis to scan at project scale.

Their study checks how well those detectors do in real use, and digs into why they fail when they fail. Lab scores on small snippets can flatter a tool badly. A clear view of root causes tells builders where to fix: the model, the analysis, or the join between them.
arxiv-2601-19439:
Giuseppe Chiari, Michele Piccoli, and Davide Zoni build data sets to teach machines the art of analog chip layout. Automating analog circuit design is a long standing challenge. Layout, parasitic effects, and circuit performance tangle in ways that are hard to capture and harder to optimize with classic methods.

Their system, OSIRIS, generates such data sets at scale, so learning methods have material to train on. Analog design still leans on scarce human experts. Machine help trained on sound, scalable data could shorten design cycles for the chips inside cars, sensors, and medical gear.
arxiv-2601-19639:
Antonio Agresti, Fabian Germ, and Mark Veraar work on stochastic partial differential equations. These equations model systems driven by random noise spread over space and time. The roughest noise is not trace class, which breaks many standard tools. Solutions are often built from Gaussian series with infinitely many terms.

The authors prove sharp bounds for such series. The bounds say exactly how the size of the sum depends on its ingredients. Sharpness means the estimates cannot be improved in general. With those bounds in hand, existence results for equations with rough noise become reachable. Applications include physical systems where the driving noise is very irregular. The work supplies a key technical step for that theory.
arxiv-2601-19939:
Hyunmin Kim and colleagues predict whole-body disease from images of the retina. The idea, called oculomics, rests on the eye's blood vessels mirroring the body's. Transformer foundation models such as RETFound made retinal prediction data-efficient. The authors build on that base with a hierarchical sampling method named Oculomix.

Their system targets systemic diseases such as cardiovascular disease and dementia. Sampling at several levels of the image hierarchy should capture both fine vessel detail and broad patterns. Cheap eye scans that flag body-wide risk could change screening. Clinics already photograph retinas routinely for eye disease. The work explores how much more those same images can say.
arxiv-2601-20039:
Vedat Levi Alev and Uriya A. First study hypergraph samplers, a tool for cutting the error of randomized algorithms. The setup uses uniform hypergraphs whose number of vertices is not too large compared with the edge size. Samplers let an algorithm repeat a weak test in a structured way so that the overall error drops.

The authors examine both typical and worst-case behavior of these samplers. The question covers decision problems with one-sided or two-sided error. Knowing where samplers help, and where they fail, guides the design of fast randomized methods in computer science theory.
arxiv-2601-20139:
Nathan Sauldubois studies model risk in finance through distributionally robust optimization with static hedging. The setting adds constraints on the marginal laws of prices and on martingale behavior, which keeps prices free of simple arbitrage. The work continues an earlier paper that left one case open.

That open case covers static hedges built from vanilla options that mature in a second period. A static hedge is set once and held, rather than traded over time. Results here help banks bound their losses when the true price model differs from the one they assumed.
arxiv-2601-20239:
Zhemeng Zhang and a large team present TouchGuide, a way to give robot policies a sense of touch at run time. Robots that handle delicate or contact-rich tasks still rely mostly on vision, and tactile feedback is often left unused. TouchGuide fuses touch with vision inside a low-dimensional action space.

The method works in two stages and steers a pretrained visuomotor policy while it runs, with no retraining. It can guide policies built on diffusion or flow-matching models. Adding touch at inference time could make existing robot policies safer on tasks like inserting, gripping, and sliding objects.
arxiv-2601-20339:
Yangyi Shen and seven colleagues improve how diffusion language models generate text. These models can build text in any order, which opens many possible paths to a finished sentence. Current decoding picks a single path and commits to it, so much of that space goes unexplored.

The authors introduce Order-Token Search, which searches jointly over the order of generation and the token values chosen. Exploring both dimensions at once should find better outputs than fixing the order in advance. Stronger decoding would help diffusion models compete with standard left-to-right models on quality.
arxiv-2601-20439:
Qihao Wang and four colleagues present PEARL, a framework that improves how language models use external tools over many steps. Models with tools can search, compute, and act, but complex multi-turn use exposes weak planning, invented tool calls, wrong parameters, and brittle interaction. PEARL joins plan exploration with adaptive reinforcement learning.

The design aims to make the model plan before acting and adjust as results come back. Multihop tool use is where agents earn their keep on real tasks, chaining lookups and actions. A stronger planner would cut the errors that now force users to supervise each step.
arxiv-2601-20539:
Oguzhan Gungordu, Siheng Xiong, and Faramarz Fekri present PathWise, a framework that uses large language models to design heuristics for hard combinatorial problems. Automated heuristic design with language models is promising, but existing frameworks lean on fixed evolutionary rules and static prompts. That leads to short-sighted heuristics, repeated evaluations, and little reasoning about how a new heuristic should be derived.

PathWise plans through a world model and lets the language models evolve themselves. Better automatic heuristics would help logistics, scheduling, and chip design, where good rules of thumb are worth large sums. Good rules of thumb save real time in each of these fields.
arxiv-2601-21239:
Chentong Chen, Mengyuan Zhong, Ye Fan, Jialong Shi, and Jianyong Sun improve how language models design search methods on their own. Models can now draft algorithms, but most tools treat the draft as one block of text. That view misses the link between the shape of a method and the numbers inside it.

Their system, TIDE, tunes the numbers while the structure evolves. Good methods are no longer thrown away just because their constants were off. The search also avoids settling too early on weak designs. Joining tuning with evolution gives the model a fairer test of each idea it creates.
arxiv-2601-21339:
Jennifer Haase and six co-authors ask what drives the quality of creative writing from language models. Outputs vary, but the cause could be the prompt, the choice of model, or plain chance in sampling. The team ran a large study to split those effects apart.

They tested a dozen models on ten creative prompts, with many samples per pairing. For originality, the prompt and the model choice explained shares of the spread that were close in size. Chance alone played a smaller role than many assume. The findings help users decide whether to switch models or rewrite the prompt when output feels stale.
arxiv-2601-21439:
Jon Chun and Katherine Elkins test whether emotional framing can sway language models in rule-bound decisions. Models are known to bend with small wording changes and to flatter user views. Whether that bend reaches high-stakes, rule-bound choices was less clear.

The authors find what they call a paradox of robustness. Despite their surface brittleness, tuned models barely moved under emotional framing. Their choices stayed nearly fixed even when the wording pushed hard. The result cuts both ways: steady rules are good, but the same firmness could lock in a bad rule. The study maps where model judgment holds firm.
arxiv-2601-21739:
Alberto Fernández-Hernández, Cristian Pérez-Corral, Jose I. Mestre, Manuel F. Dolz, and Enrique S. Quintana-Ortí explain an odd fact about the Adam optimizer. Adam has powered large-scale training for nearly a decade. Users kept noticing that setting its two momentum parameters equal works better, in scores and in the feel of training runs.

No principle accounted for that fact. The authors name a missing gradient scale invariance principle behind it. When the two parameters match, the updates respect that invariance. A clear principle turns a folk trick into a rule builders can apply on purpose, and it may guide the design of the next optimizer.
arxiv-2601-21839:
Ander Artola Velasco and co-authors study a new market dynamic created by reasoning models. Giving a language model more compute at test time improves its reasoning. But cloud providers charge users for that compute, so better answers now come with metered bills.

That pricing turns reasoning into a game among providers and users, each with their own incentives. The team's 2026 preprint frames these interactions as test-time compute games and analyzes them. The framing matters because the economics will shape how much reasoning users actually buy, how providers set prices. And whether careful thinking becomes a luxury feature. Game theory offers tools to predict where such a market settles before it fully forms.
arxiv-2601-22139:
Xin Chen and co-authors teach reasoning models to ask questions. Reasoning language models have advanced through chain-of-thought prompting, yet they share a blind habit. They reason at length inside their own heads even when key information is missing or ambiguous. The authors call this blind self-thinking.

Esteban Macías, Ilya Gruzberg, and Eldad Bettelheim solve the spin quantum Hall transition on random networks with exact exponents. audubon-ornithological-biography-vol5-18:
With volume five in 1839, Audubon completed the text of his Ornithological Biography. The five volumes stand beside The Birds of America as its prose half. Final species accounts fill the volume in his established manner. Habits, ranges, nests, and notes from the field make up each life history.

Audubon drew on journeys that had taken him across much of North America. His frontier tales give the science a human frame of hardship and wonder. The completed set remains a primary record of American bird life before heavy settlement. Later bird students mined it for early ranges and habits. The whole work is a monument to one observer.
awntyrs-arthure-madden-1839:
The Awntyrs off Arthure is a Middle English poem in the alliterative style, edited by Frederic Madden in 1839. Its scene is a hunt near Carlisle, in the border country of Arthur's realm. Few Arthurian poems mix splendor and horror as boldly as this one does.

Gawain and Queen Guinevere meet the rotting ghost of the queen's own mother. The dead woman warns them against pride, luxury, and the price both will pay. Her words hang over the court's bright feast like smoke. The poem then turns to a knightly duel, but the ghost's warning is what readers remember. It is Arthurian horror at its finest.
carle-of-carlisle-madden-1839:
The Carle of Carlisle is a Middle English romance edited by Frederic Madden in 1839. A carle is a rough, churlish fellow, and this one keeps a hall near Carlisle. Gawain, Kay, and a bishop ride there and must spend the night as his guests.

The host tests his guests' manners at every turn, at table and even at bedtime. Kay fails rudely, as Kay usually does. Gawain passes each test with patience and good grace. The comedy turns on a plain point: courtesy is a knight's real armor. Madden's edition kept this brisk, funny tale in print for modern readers of Arthur.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-james-beaton-: This 1913 reference article on the elder Beaton — Archbishop of St. Andrews. Oswald Hunter-Blair honors his mighty primacy. He faced the Lutheran tempest. Scotland knew the princely name. The last of the medieval primates. His 1539 death is famed.
cia-0000008639:
Quang Binh province is the setting for a November 1972 report on two dead pilots sighted there. Quang Binh, just north of the old demilitarized zone, endured some of the war's heaviest bombing. Reports of dead airmen arrived as the bombing campaign neared its end.

Such reports served the accounting effort rather than rescue, fixing where losses had occurred. A place name could let officials match remains or graves to missing crews later. The work was grim, and its results often stayed incomplete. Still, each filed sighting narrowed the unknown for two men's families and records alike.
cia-0000009439:
Two subjects share a February 1971 CIA report: sightings of American prisoners, and a Viet Cong prisoner of war camp. The camp heading names a military region in shortened form, cut off in the surviving title. Pairing sightings with a camp suggests the men and the place were linked.

Combined reports helped analysts place captives inside a system, not just on a map. A camp's location could explain a cluster of sightings around it. The file therefore works at two levels at once: individual men, and the network holding them. That double view was the heart of prisoner intelligence work.
cia-0000010239:
Keeping a beachhead in South Korea, and what that would mean worldwide, is weighed in a January 1951 CIA paper. United Nations forces then held a perimeter around Pusan after months of retreat, and Chinese troops had entered the war. Withdrawal or holding fast was a live question.

The paper looks past the battlefield to allies, enemies, and neutrals watching America's resolve. A beachhead kept or lost would speak far beyond Korea, to Europe and Asia alike. Such strategic papers show the young CIA arguing at the highest level. This one captures the Korean War's darkest winter from Washington's side.
cia-0000013239:
The enemy prison order of battle in Laos is estimated in a CIA paper from July 1969. Order of battle means the count of units and their strength. Here the units counted are the camps of the secret war. The estimate tallies their staffs, their guards, and the men believed held in the Laotian camps scattered through the hills.

The Laotian camps were the secret war's hidden archipelago of suffering. Counting their keepers was grim, necessary work for the accounting. For readers, the estimate shows the prison system measured like an army, because in Laos it nearly was one.
cia-0000013839:
American prisoners were put on exhibition by their captors, and a CIA item from February 1967 records the displays. The enemy paraded captives before cameras and crowds for propaganda value. The exhibitions were meant for foreign eyes above all else. They offered proof of the prisoners' existence to the world. They also pressed on the government that had sent the men, staged as theater in the war for opinion.

The item notes the parades as the files watched the watchers. Names and faces in such displays fed the accounting back home. For readers, the page shows captivity used as a stage, with prisoners as unwilling actors.
cia-0000013939: Two American soldiers were captured in Darlac Province, in a CIA note dated February 1, 1968. Darlac sat in the central highlands of South Vietnam. Ground troops there fought far from the coast and its support. The note records the pair's capture at the start of a hard year in the highlands war.
cia-0000014639: Communist matters is the heading over a CIA file on Russell Alton McNutt, dated August 6, 1951. The file gives the results of an interview with McNutt. Interviews were the slow grind of the spy hunt, name by name. This file adds one talk to the thick record the hunt built around a single man.
cia-0000015339: Flying Saucers is the title of a CIA file dated September 4, 1952. A memo is attached, dated September 24, on the same subject. The fall of 1952 followed the summer's great wave of sightings. Memos stacked on memos as offices tried to fix a line on the strange reports. The saucer file and its memo are held in the CIA Reading Room.
cia-0000022339: Commentary headed simply Gary Powers fills a CIA record dated July 2, 1960. A one word label gives the reader nothing but the subject, and this account adds nothing the title lacks. The Powers trial was then weeks away in Moscow. Even bare commentary clippings were saved, since the agency was tracking every shade of world opinion on the case.
cia-0000036539:
A CIA daily report on Latin America from August 1977 rounds up news from across the region. Among its items, Bolivia calls Peru's auto program proposal unacceptable. Daily reports of this kind turned wire news into a single brief for officials.

The report moves from country to country, giving each story a few lines and no more. An item on car making sits beside politics, which was normal for these daily sweeps. They remain a handy snapshot of what one day's news looked like to the agency. Bolivia's remark also shows how even trade and industry policy drew the agency's daily eye.
cia-0000036639:
Photo comparison results from Christmas 1969 name William Johnson, in a CIA record dated January 2, 1971. The analysis belongs to the MIA and POW identification effort. Johnson's case was worked from the same holiday photographs used in many other cases. The Christmas set of images, released by Hanoi, was the best visual evidence the searchers had that year.

The record holds the analysts' findings for this one serviceman's file. Set beside the other Johnson result in the files, it shows how cases were revisited as work went on. Repetition was part of the process, since a second look could catch what the first look missed in a crowded photograph.
cia-0000042739:
A university group condemned the Salvadoran killings, in a CIA record dated October 2, 1989 in the catalog. The killings at the heart of the outcry were those of the Jesuit priests. They had been teachers at the university in San Salvador.

Inside, the group's protest against the murders is preserved as issued. Universities spoke with a special claim here, since the dead were scholars. The file shows the academic world answering violence against its own. Statements like this one kept the victims' work, not only their deaths, in front of the public as the case unfolded.
cia-0000044039:
Daniel Ortega condemned the Jesuits' assassination, in a CIA record dated October 5, 1989 in the catalog. Ortega was Nicaragua's president and a leader of the Sandinista movement. His country and El Salvador stood on the same side of the region's wars.

Inside, the Nicaraguan leader's rebuke of the killings is preserved. Condemnation from Managua carried weight across Central America. It also served Nicaragua in its long contest with Washington. The file shows the murders drawing in the whole region, as each government used the crime to press its own case in the court of world opinion.
cia-0000044439:
Cristiani spoke on military involvement in the killings, in a CIA record dated October 1, 1989 in the catalog. Military involvement was the question at the case's very center. A president's words on it bound him in public from that day.

Inside, the president's careful statement on his army's role is preserved. Admissions in such cases are usually measured out in small parts. What he conceded, and what he left unsaid, both mattered greatly. The file lets readers take that measure themselves, with the statement whole before them, as officials in many capitals first read it that autumn.
cia-0000049039: The director of El Salvador's National Police felt relief in 1982 at a move by the minister of defense. A CIA item from that year records the moment. The Caribbean situation fills a CIA briefing prepared for the National Security Council. The briefing is dated June 3, 1959. It came five months after Fidel Castro's victory in Cuba had shaken the whole region and its governments.

Inside, analysts survey unrest and political change across the island chain. Cuba's example was encouraging rebels and worrying friendly governments at the same time. The Caribbean had become Washington's most unsettled neighborhood almost overnight. For readers, the briefing shows how widely American officials were looking for the next crisis. It dates from the months when Castro's win was still new and its effects were still spreading.

The document tracks the plan and the reports behind it. In the end Khrushchev never made the journey to the island. Even so, the plan itself was major news in Washington. For readers, the entry shows how seriously a rumored visit was taken. It also marks how close Moscow and Havana already seemed by the spring of 1960.

crania-americana-or-a-comparative-view-o: Crania Americana of 1839 compared skulls of native peoples. The American crania. The comparative anatomy. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care for all readers. The archive keeps the paper open to all who seek it.
dreams-pg1439: Olive Schreiner's 1890 book of allegories: dream-visions about life, death, labor, and women's lot, written in biblical, poetic prose. "The Hunter" and other parables made her a prophet to a generation of reformers. Strange, beautiful, and fiercely moral.
europmc-pmc10163139:
Kautzky-Willer, Leutner, and Harreiter review sex differences in type 2 diabetes in a 2023 paper. Diabetes is rising in both sexes, but men tend to be diagnosed younger and at lower body fat than women. Worldwide, millions more men than women live with the disease, while women often carry a heavier load of risk factors at diagnosis.

The review compares causes, complications, and treatment responses in men and women. It argues that care and prevention should account for these differences. The paper is a compact guide to a topic long treated as one-size-fits-all.
europmc-pmc10180739:
Fusco and colleagues review gut bacteria that produce short-chain fatty acids in a 2023 paper. These fatty acids are made when gut microbes ferment fiber from food. They feed the gut lining, calm inflammation, and help control metabolism, and their shortage is linked to bowel disease, colon cancer, and heart and metabolic disorders.

The review names the key bacterial producers and the foods that feed them. It explains what the acids do in the gut and the wider body. It also weighs probiotic and diet strategies to raise their levels.
europmc-pmc10273039:
Abd-Alrazaq and co-authors review large language models in medical education in a 2023 paper, covering opportunities, challenges, and future directions. Models in the GPT family can answer questions, explain concepts, and draft text in a natural style. Medical schools are weighing how such tools change the way students learn and are tested.

Drawing on past reviews, the authors set out the gains schools might see, from personal tutoring to faster feedback. They also face the risks: wrong answers, bias, and threats to honest assessment. The paper offers a balanced guide for educators.
europmc-pmc10353939:
Bellaver and a large team asked in 2023 why some brains with amyloid do not go on to form tau tangles. Amyloid and tau are the two hallmark proteins of Alzheimer's disease. Some people carry amyloid yet stay sharp and show no tau harm. Astrocytes are star-shaped support cells in the brain that can switch to an active state.

Bellaver studied 1,016 people across three groups who had no memory loss. Amyloid linked to raised tau in blood only in people whose astrocytes were active. Brain scans showed the same split for tau growth over time. The finding puts active astrocytes early in the chain of the disease. It may help pick the right people for early drug trials.
europmc-pmc10390339:
The GBD 2021 Sickle Cell Disease Collaborators tracked the global toll of sickle cell disease from 2000 to 2021. The disease warps red blood cells into a stiff sickle shape. It passes from parents to children through genes. The study spans 204 nations and areas and counts births, cases, and deaths.

Births of babies with the disease rose 13.7%, to 515,000 in 2021. Growth was driven by population gains in the Caribbean and sub-Saharan Africa. People living with the disease rose 41.4%, to 7.74 million. Death records alone put deaths at 34,400 in 2021. The team warns that this count misses many deaths and understates the true burden.
europmc-pmc10502239:
Muzellec and colleagues built PyDESeq2 in 2023, a Python version of a key gene analysis flow. The flow tests which genes change between two sample groups in bulk RNA data. The original tool, DESeq2, lives in the R language. Many labs now work in Python, and no native tool fit this task.

Their rebuild gives near-matching results with a better fit score, Muzellec reports. It also runs faster on large data sets, as shown on cancer atlas data. The code is free under the MIT licence on GitHub. It joins the scverse family of Python tools for cell data. Users gain clean links to modern data science stacks.
europmc-pmc1238739:
Zamarin and colleagues traced how a flu protein kills cells in 2005. The protein, PB1-F2, is a small part of influenza virus. It settles in mitochondria, the energy hubs of cells. Earlier work showed it triggers cell death, but the route was unclear.

Cells with the protein reacted more strongly to death signals. Tests on mouse liver mitochondria showed a key protein leaking out. The viral protein bound two gate proteins in mitochondrial walls. Those gates control what passes between cell compartments. Zamarin links those contacts to the death effect.
europmc-pmc1240439:
Eriksson, Jakobsson, and Fredriksson asked if flame retardants harm the developing brain in 2001. These chemicals spread through goods like electronics and textiles. They persist and build up, much like older banned pollutants. Levels in breast milk were rising at the time.

Newborn mice got single doses of two common PBDE types. A third flame retardant was tested the same way. Doses were given at day ten, a key brain growth stage. Later behavior tests checked for lasting harm. Eriksson raises concern that these chemicals act as developmental neurotoxicants. Behavior was checked in the adult mice later on.
europmc-pmc1288039:
Fowler and co-authors discovered a working amyloid inside mammal tissue in 2006. Amyloid fibers are protein clumps tied to Alzheimer and Parkinson disease. They were assumed to be purely harmful accidents. A pigment cell protein changed that picture.

The protein Pmel17 forms amyloid that templates melanin production. Melanin protects against ultraviolet light and oxidative damage. The amyloid also traps toxic melanin building blocks safely. Cells orchestrate its formation through membrane and cutting steps. Fowler proves amyloid is a normal fold used from bacteria to humans. Sequestration inside the organelle guards the host cell meanwhile.
europmc-pmc1395339:
Yuan, Reed, Chen, and Stewart compared statistics for real-time PCR data in 2006. Real-time PCR is used across biomedical science. Sound statistical treatment for its data was lacking. Confidence intervals and significance were often left implicit.

Four analysis approaches were built and compared head to head. One uses multiple regression to derive the standard fold-change measure. A second uses covariance analysis for the same quantity. Two simpler routes apply group tests after a first calculation step. SAS programs were written for all four models. A data quality control model was added.
europmc-pmc1779539:
Ekman and colleagues asked in 2006 what sets hub proteins apart in baker's yeast. In the protein interaction network, most proteins touch only a few partners. Hubs are the rare proteins with very many partners. The yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae has about 6,000 proteins and tens of thousands of links.

The team compared hubs with non-hubs across the known network. Hubs turned out to be enriched for proteins built from many domains, which are reusable folding units within a protein. Hubs also often carried the same domain repeated several times. Earlier work had shown hub proteins are roughly three times as likely to be vital for survival. The domain pattern gives a concrete trait that marks these highly connected proteins.
europmc-pmc1802739:
Pahel, Rozier and Slade developed in 2007 a short scale that measures how tooth problems affect preschool children and their families. Dental disease and its treatment can lower daily quality of life, yet no tested tool existed for very young children. Their scale is called ECOHIS, short for Early Childhood Oral Health Impact Scale.

Experts first judged a pool of 45 candidate items, and parents then rated which mattered for preschoolers. The final scale kept 13 items, nine about the child and four about the family. It was tested on 295 parents of five-year-olds, plus 46 parents for repeat testing. Scores were worse when parents rated the child's health as fair or poor, or when dental disease was present. Consistency scores were high, at 0.91 for the child section and 0.95 for the family section.
europmc-pmc1847839:
Dunbar, Moran and co-authors pinned an aphid's heat tolerance in 2007 on a single DNA letter change in the bacteria living inside it. Pea aphids depend on the bacterium Buchnera, which feeds them essential nutrients. The change sits in a promoter, the switch region, for a small heat-shock protein gene named ibpA.

The deletion shortens a run of repeated letters and nearly wipes out the gene's heat response. It also lowers expression at cool and mild temperatures. After brief heat exposure as juveniles, aphids with the short form produced few or no offspring and held almost no Buchnera. In constant cool conditions those same aphids bred earlier and kept higher fertility. The mutation recurs in lab lines and occurs in field populations, trading heat safety for cool-weather gain.
europmc-pmc2008239:
Tannock studied in 1968 how cell growth in a mouse tumour relates to its blood vessels. Tissues need vessels for nutrients, so cells near vessels may divide faster. Most tumours are too tangled for this test. The transplanted mammary tumour used here grew in cords of living tissue around fairly straight vessels, with dead tissue beyond.

Most cords had radii between 60 and 120 micrometres. The central vessels averaged about 9.5 micrometres in radius, and cord size did not change with tumour weight. Cells near vessels showed high protein making and rapid proliferation. Growth fell with distance from the vessel. Tannock concluded that oxygen likely controls growth mainly through the growth fraction, the share of cells actively dividing.
europmc-pmc2034139:
Thomsen and colleagues measured nitric oxide production in human breast tumours in 1995. Nitric oxide is a small signalling molecule made by enzymes called nitric oxide synthases. The team had already found these enzymes in gynaecological cancers. Here they assessed enzyme activity and nitric oxide output in breast tumours and in normal breast tissue, and located the enzymes by staining.

Both calcium-dependent and calcium-independent enzyme activity ran high in invasive tumours. Nitric oxide output was also higher than in benign or normal tissue. For invasive ductal cancers, output was significantly greater in grade III tumours than grade II, linking it to tumour grade. Staining placed the inducible enzyme mainly in macrophages, immune cells gathered around the tumour. Other staining appeared in blood vessel and muscle-like cells.
