No motor drilled past the canal's end. All three approaches landed within the accepted tolerance about equally often. Still, the standalone sensor's canals ended closest to the ideal point. Both motor groups finished similarly to each other. For dentists, the message is reassuring but nuanced. Built-in sensors are safe, though a separate measurement may hold the endpoint slightly truer.
plos-pone-0356139: He and one co-author published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on reading stock market reactions with large models. They paired large language or AI models with time series forecasting tools. The aim was to judge how markets respond to news or events. Blending text-savvy models with price history may sharpen market analysis, a task where timing and tone both move money.
plos-pone-0356239:
Amjad Bani Hani and seven colleagues compare two ways of counting antibiotic use in a Jordanian hospital's intensive care units, in this 2026 study. Stewardship programs track antibiotics to fight resistance, but the standard measures can disagree. One counts standardized daily doses set by the World Health Organization; the other simply counts each day a patient receives a drug. The team pulled a year of records for just over six hundred ICU patients who received antimicrobials.

The two measures tracked each other closely overall, yet differed meaningfully for individual drugs. Counting treatment days, the authors argue, gives clinicians a clearer picture of how long patients are actually exposed in intensive care, where doses are often adjusted. Standardized doses remain better for comparing hospitals. Their conclusion is that the measures complement each other and should not be treated as interchangeable.
plos-pone-0356539:
Christopher Whelpley and three others test whether standard hiring tools treat autistic applicants fairly, in this 2026 study. Interviews are known to disadvantage autistic candidates, so employers often turn to tests as the objective alternative. The researchers gave autistic and neurotypical adults three widely used selection tools, covering general mental ability, personality, and situational judgment, situations in which applicants choose what they would do at work.

All three tools produced real score gaps against autistic adults. That gap persisted even with ability held equal, personality, age, and gender. The authors caution this is early work, but the pattern suggests that tests billed as neutral can carry the same adverse impact as interviews. They call for hiring methods built to capture job-relevant strengths in neurodiverse applicants rather than quietly screening them out.
plos-pone-0356739:
Jaqueline S Angelo and colleagues added a smart alert layer to SISS-Geo, Brazil's free wildlife health reporting platform. The platform has collected georeferenced reports from professionals and the public since 2014. Their 2026 paper introduces the Z-Alert index. Reports are first grouped into clusters in space and time. Each cluster is then scored on weighted factors. These include the share of dead animals, the time span, and the geographic spread.

Weights were tuned by optimization, and managers can adjust the thresholds that trigger action. The team validated the system against historical Brazilian yellow fever data from the health ministry. That is a fitting test, since the disease spills from wildlife to people. Sharper alerts help surveillance teams spend scarce investigation budgets where an outbreak is likeliest.
plos-pone-0358039:
Zhiyue Xu and partners published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE on whether stomach infection with Helicobacter pylori goes with high uric acid, a condition tied to gout. The bacterium has been linked to metabolic troubles beyond the stomach, but earlier studies were small and often ignored body weight and kidney function. Drawing on a huge health examination database of close to sixty-eight thousand adults, they adjusted step by step for metabolic, kidney, and inflammation factors.

At first glance the link looked clear: infected people had more high uric acid. But each adjustment layer shrank it, until in the fullest model the association was tiny and statistically uncertain. A very small rise in uric acid levels remained, and patterns held for men and women separately. Most of the apparent connection, they conclude, reflects the company infection keeps, body size and metabolic health, rather than a strong effect of the bacterium.
plos-pone-0358239:
Quynh Hoa Truong and Xuan Khanh Truong show that a nanoparticle's surface floppiness can flip how cells respond to its charge, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Charge is the usual dial for predicting whether immune cells swallow a nanocarrier. The authors instead measured the diversity of shapes the particle's surface ligands can adopt, an information based score. They scored one hundred five gold nanoparticles from a benchmark dataset. Then they watched the charge rule break at a threshold.

Below the threshold, more positive charge meant more uptake, as textbooks say. Above it, the relationship reversed: charge predicted less uptake, consistent with floppy ligands shielding the surface. Adding the entropy score improved prediction across several model types, with the gains concentrated in the floppy regime. A second dataset of over six hundred mixed particles supported the pattern. Drug designers gain a descriptor that tells them when their dial stops working.
plos-pone-0358439:
Bhavana Rhythm and three colleagues translate and validate a listening effort questionnaire for Kannada speakers with hearing loss, in PLOS ONE in 2026. The Extended Effort Assessment Scale measures how hard people must strain to follow speech, a burden hearing tests miss. No checked version existed for Kannada, a major language of southern India. The team translated the scale both ways, reviewed it with experts, and tested it on one hundred native speaking adults.

Nine of the ten items behaved well in statistical checks; the telephone item misfitted, likely because phone listening mixes several demands at once. Overall consistency and repeat reliability were excellent, and scores tracked a simple effort rating scale as expected. Two items behaved differently by age or gender, so the authors advise care comparing those across groups. Clinicians now have a tested Kannada tool for a complaint patients voice often.
plos-pone-0358539:
Matthieu Lebrat leads a team of six measuring what happens to prescriptions when a hospital's specialists review them together, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Multi professional medication reviews bring doctors, pharmacists, and nurses around one table to prune drug lists, and psychiatry, where patients often carry heavy sedative loads, had little evidence. The French university hospital study compared stays before and after reviews began across four psychiatric wards, spanning 2017 to 2023.

After reviews started, patients left hospital with about one fewer prescribed drug on average, a small but statistically firm shift. The cuts concentrated where they matter most: psychotropic medicines fell furthest, led by benzodiazepines, with antipsychotics and anticholinergic drugs also down, and even laxatives, often prescribed to counter drug side effects, declined. No drug class rose to compensate. The authors read the pattern as reviews doing quiet, compounding good in a high risk prescribing environment.
plos-pone-0358739: Mumtaz and three co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on how two small RNA molecules tune a gene that drives blood vessel growth. The gene, ERG, is a transcription factor for vessel lining cells. The two regulators are named miR-6756 and miR-3190. Knowing which small RNAs dial a vessel gene up or down can guide work on diseases where vessel growth helps or harms.
plos-pone-0358839:
Manal Nhili leads a team of eight measuring how fast a devastating goat disease spreads through a herd, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Peste des petits ruminants sweeps through goats and sheep in much of Africa and Asia, and control plans need hard numbers on transmission. The researchers infected goats experimentally while ultra wideband collars logged the distance between every pair of animals minute by minute, alongside clinical and virus checks.

Density proved decisive. At low density a healthy goat needed nearly two days of exposure near sick animals to catch the virus; packed tightly, four hours sufficed. Each infectious goat was estimated to infect roughly four to nine others, depending on how long it stayed contagious, and incubation ran about two weeks. Crowded livestock markets stand out as danger points where brief mixing can seed outbreaks across regions.
plos-pone-0359339: Sun and four co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE paper on turning Chinese Braille documents into text. Their decoding method is aware of uncertainty, so it can weigh doubtful readings instead of forcing a guess. The structure of the document guides those choices. Better transcription opens printed material to blind readers and helps digitize Braille archives that now sit unscanned.
plos-pone-0359439:
Yuanyuan Tang and colleagues examined in 2026 how changing land use has reshaped the movement of carbon through soils in northern China. Soil holds enormous amounts of carbon, and converting land between farming, grassland, and forest changes how much carbon the soil stores or releases. The study focuses on that region's soil carbon dynamics under such changes.

Tang and co-authors trace how the shifts in land use altered carbon inputs, storage, and loss over time. Their subject sits at the crossing of farming practice and climate policy, since soil carbon is one of the largest levers in the land carbon budget. Findings of this kind inform decisions about which land conversions help climate goals and which quietly undo them.
plos-pone-0359639:
Masawa Nyamuryekung'e, Kokila Lakhoo, and Salome Maswime published this protocol in PLOS ONE in 2026. It sets out a study protocol, in several phases with mixed methods, assessing whether Tanzania's health system can care for babies born with major structural defects. The tracer condition is anorectal malformations, birth defects of the bowel opening that need early surgery.

A tracer condition stands in for a wider service: if the system handles this defect well, it likely handles similar newborn surgery too. Assessing surgeons, equipment, and referral paths shows where children born with defects lose their chance of timely care. Tanzanian health planners and children's surgery teams are the audience.
pmc-13238239:
Zhou and colleagues vaccinate mice against toxoplasmosis using DNA that codes for two parasite proteins. Toxoplasma gondii lives inside cells and infects nearly all warm-blooded animals, people included. No human vaccine exists. The two target proteins, TgGRA47 and TgGRA72, are shed by the parasite inside its host cell and help shape its survival there.

The team gave BALB/c mice DNA vaccines carrying each protein's gene, then challenged them with the parasite. They measured immune responses and survival to judge protection. A DNA vaccine that works in mice offers a cheap, stable platform worth refining, since toxoplasmosis endangers unborn babies and people with weak immunity worldwide.
pmc-13240639:
Huang and co-workers at Jilin University tested Nintendo Switch exergaming as support for adults with subthreshold depression. Such mild symptoms raise the risk of full depression, yet exercise habits are hard to sustain. Eighty-four adults joined a randomized trial with interviews afterward. Half played active games two or three times weekly for eight weeks.

The gaming group did better on depressive symptoms at every follow-up through week sixteen. Sleep quality also got much better, and anxiety eased at several points. Interviews with seventeen players told of immersion and habits that helped them stick with it. No adverse events took place, and the authors pitch commercial exergames as accessible early support.
pmc-13242339:
Okhamafe's team in Tel Aviv showed that changing 'ten' moves effort ratings in set directions. 26 trained adults performed isometric holds across three moves. Force ran from light to all-out. Effort was rated against three anchors: the same task's max, another task's max, or a personal lifetime max. Sessions rotated the three anchors in mixed order.

Task-matched anchors kept producing the highest ratings; self-set anchors the lowest. Gaps widened near maximal force, at eighty to one hundred percent effort. Rankings survived every anchor tested, keeping rough scale match. The team urges clear anchor rules in training research and coaching practice.
pmc-13242439:
Sakine Yılmaz and colleagues examined how stressful gender expectations relate to mental distress in women treated for breast cancer in Türkiye. Their study appeared in Supportive Care in Cancer in 2026. It surveyed 264 women who attended a state hospital's surgical oncology clinic after mastectomy. Because the breast is tied to feminine identity and body image, the team expected the stress of gender expectations to weigh on mental health after surgery.

Both gender role stress and distress ran high in this group. Women with university degrees, those in nuclear families, and those whose husbands held degrees reported especially high levels of both. Surprisingly, gender role stress itself was not significantly linked to distress in the analysis. The authors still urge nurses to assess both together, along with coping strategies, when caring for women after mastectomy. The findings show distress after this surgery has social roots, not only medical ones.
pmc-13244139:
Tristan Burgess and co-authors report a case where bedside ultrasound sped the diagnosis of an ischemic finger. Their case report appeared in Clinical Case Reports in 2026. A finger starved of blood can come from clots on either side of the circulation, and the cause decides the cure. Point-of-care ultrasound let the team check arteries and veins directly at the bedside, without waiting for formal imaging, and to map how far the blockage reached.

The workup landed on a rare double diagnosis. The patient carried two clotting disorders at once: polycythemia vera, a blood cancer that thickens the blood with extra red cells, and antiphospholipid syndrome, an autoimmune clotting condition. Each alone can explain a blocked digit; together they compounded the danger. The authors remind clinicians to keep both on the checklist for limb ischemia. Rare pairs do occur, and missing one leaves half the problem untreated.
pmc-13245839:
León-Herrera and co-authors reviewed digital health tools for the mental and thinking problems of long COVID, in this 2026 scoping review. Long COVID often leaves people with brain fog, anxiety, depression, and fatigue, while specialist care is scarce. The reviewers searched four databases for studies of app-based and online programs aimed at these symptoms.

From nearly nine hundred records, only twenty-five studies qualified, most testing multi-part programs that combined exercises such as cognitive training, therapy, and symptom tracking. Results pointed to promise, especially for combined programs, but the evidence stayed preliminary, with few strong trials. The authors call for randomized studies, standard outcome measures, and attention to digital access.
pmc-13247039:
Gandjour evaluated Germany's drug stockpiling law in this 2026 Scientific Reports health-economics study. A recent legal change made six-month inventory reserves the government's main defense against medicine shortages. Working from the German social health insurance perspective, the author examined a public database of nearly two thousand eight hundred recorded shortages since 2012. The author modeled how many a reserve of a given length could have prevented.

A six-month reserve would have prevented roughly seventy percent of shortages. Each extra month prevented fewer additional shortages, so value for money thinned as stockpiles lengthened, with an estimated cost-effective ceiling near two and a half years under stated assumptions. The author concludes the six-month mandate is very likely cost-effective, while flagging warehouse practices as a key uncertainty.
pmc-13248739:
Nguyen and co-authors describe a rare surgical emergency in this 2026 case report. A sixty-two-year-old woman was having an infected keloid scar removed when she began bleeding uncontrollably during the operation. Tests confirmed disseminated intravascular coagulation, a dangerous state where clotting runs wild and then leaves the blood unable to clot.

Her preoperative clotting tests had been normal, though the scar had been inflamed for years. Doctors gave blood products, strong antibiotics, and kidney support, and her clotting recovered within fourteen hours. She recovered fully. The authors warn that chronic infected tissue can, rarely, trigger this crisis mid-surgery, and that fast teamwork saves lives.
pmc-13250839:
Adel Alsharei and a large team report a double gene puzzle in this 2026 case report. A seven-year-old Syrian boy kept breaking bones and had marked facial features pointing to a rare growth disorder called geleophysic dysplasia.

Scans and standard lab tests were mostly normal, though his bone density matched that of a 92-year-old. Gene testing found two altered copies of a gene called LTBP3, tied to this disorder. It also found one altered copy of a collagen gene, linked to a different condition he does not seem to show. His fractures were treated with casts and surgery. The team backs gene testing for children with repeated breaks.
pmc-13252039:
Kristianto and colleagues group patients by metabolic and body profiles linked to the ankle-brachial index, a leg blood flow test. Their 2026 Vascular Health and Risk Management study covers more than one thousand people seen at clinics and hospitals around Malang, Indonesia, between 2023 and 2025. Thirteen measures, from blood pressure to body composition, fed the analysis.

A k-means algorithm split the group into two clusters, running from healthier profiles to high cardiometabolic risk. Trimming the inputs to seven features sharpened the grouping, with belly fat, resting metabolism, and body mass leading. The authors stress the clusters describe patterns rather than diagnoses or predictions. They suggest the approach could help nurses and clinicians think about leg circulation risk, pending validation.
pmc-13254339:
Mohammed Ali and co-authors solve a wave equation for optical fibers in a 2026 mathematics study. Their model is a high-order stochastic nonlinear Schrödinger equation, which describes how solitons, self-keeping wave pulses, travel in fibers under noise and higher-order effects. They used a wave transformation and a mapping method with symbolic computing.

The method produced many exact solutions, including bright, dark, singular, periodic, and rational soliton types. A stability analysis showed the solutions stay stable under small disturbances. Graphs under varied settings display the dynamics, and the authors say the method handles this equation class reliably.
pmc-13261039:
Julia S Etkin and Vincent Joralemon wrote a 2026 legal analysis of who bears liability when AI chatbots give bad prescribing advice. Chatbots increasingly give patients prescribing-level guidance without a physician involved. The authors discuss the learned intermediary doctrine. That rule has long governed drug makers' duty to warn through doctors. They argue it operates differently in two emerging pathways: AI working behind the clinician, and AI advising patients directly, with no intermediary at all.

They cite studies in which ChatGPT wrongly reported no interaction between Paxlovid and verapamil, a dangerous error, and gave incomplete or wrong answers to nearly three-quarters of drug questions. Surveys show about a fifth of United States adults have used ChatGPT for health information, and nearly a third of those changed medications based on it. The authors warn clinicians may need to screen patients for AI-sourced prescribing advice under ordinary malpractice law.
pmc-13263139:
Francesco Compagnoni and Michele A Riva revisit a nineteenth-century Italian doctor's experiments on sugar and tooth decay in a 2026 historical article. Paolo Mantegazza, a physician and anthropologist, addressed the question in his 1864 hygiene manual, one of Italy's most influential public health books. People had long blamed sugar for rotten teeth, but the mechanism was disputed.

Mantegazza tested whether sugar chemically attacks tooth enamel in the laboratory. He concluded sugar does no direct chemical harm, and that damage instead comes from fermentation, in which microbes break sugar down. That reading anticipated the modern germ-based account of decay by decades. The authors credit his hands-on method and his push to spread science for public health.
pmc-13263339:
Helene Ackermann and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on how failure feedback from a robot tutor affects adult learners in real time. Ninety adults aged eighteen to fifty-nine completed a learning task. A humanoid robot gave feedback in three styles: fixed, frequency-adaptive, or personalized to each learner's errors.

Both thinking-focused and planning-focused failure feedback raised the chance of a correct next answer in all three styles. Making feedback frequency-adaptive added no clear benefit. Personalized content weakened the instant effect of thinking-focused feedback yet improved overall performance. Learners with higher ability gained less from the feedback, while those feeling bored in the moment gained more.
pmc-13263539:
Noah S. Brown and co-authors present a 2026 case report with a literature review on a rare spread of a pancreatic growth into the belly cavity. A 65-year-old woman had a large cyst in the tail of her pancreas, a mucus-producing tumor called an IPMN. She underwent removal of the pancreatic tail and spleen.

During surgery, doctors found two separate deposits of cell-free mucin in her pelvis. That pattern is pseudomyxoma peritonei, a condition where mucin collects in the abdomen, usually from appendix or ovarian tumors. Pancreatic cases are extremely rare, reported only nineteen times before. Both deposits were removed, she recovered well, and the authors recommend expert centers and scan-based follow-up.
pmc-13263639:
Ting Zhao and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on a natural compound, D-chiral inositol, in rats modeling polycystic ovary syndrome. This common hormone disorder disrupts ovulation and metabolism. The compound is known to help insulin work better. The team induced the syndrome with letrozole, then treated the rats for four weeks.

Treatment improved the polycystic ovary appearance and normalized sex hormone and insulin levels. Gene-expression profiling showed significant changes in genes including Lamc2, Inhba, and Bdkrb2. Targeted chemical profiling confirmed that amino acid metabolism, the handling of protein building blocks, also improved. The authors describe the compound's effect as multi-target and body-wide rather than limited to a single pathway.
pmc-13263739:
Zelong Tang and colleagues test a plant coumarin as a guard for brain stem cells after stroke-like injury. Bergapten, from the furanocoumarin family, already shows signs of fighting oxidative damage and swelling. Their 2026 lab study mimics the hostile zone around a stroke with hydrogen peroxide on mouse cells.

Peroxide flooded neural stem cells with reactive oxygen and drove many to die, while pushing microglia toward their attack mode. Bergapten fought the oxidative stress and calmed the inflammation in their assays. Guarded stem cells lived on better and chose nerve-cell fates more readily under stress. The authors frame the compound as a hope for mending the stroke-damaged brain's own nursery.
pmc-13264439:
Fazeela Bibi and a large team present a 2026 case report on colon cancer in a child, a very rare event. The cancer type, adenocarcinoma, is common in adults but almost unheard of in children. Its vague signs often lead to late care, so single cases carry lessons.

Their patient was a 10-year-old boy with belly pain, constipation, and rectal bleeding for three months. A scope exam found a narrowed, ulcer-like growth in the sigmoid colon, the last part of the large bowel. Lab study showed a poorly formed cancer with signet-ring cells, a harsh type. The cancer had not spread. Surgeons removed the affected part, and the boy recovered well. The authors urge early scope checks for such signs.
pmc-13264939:
Miriyala Gaayathri and co-authors published a 2026 study on improving how trainee emergency doctors document bedside ultrasound scans in a busy Indian emergency department. Poor records weaken care and teaching. The team used theory-guided steps over 19 months, including teaching, co-design, workflow fixes, and feedback rounds.

They assessed 3,074 scans. At the start, no scans met 80 percent of the national documentation standard, and the median score was 24 percent. After the program, 35.1 percent of scans passed the bar and the median score rose to 69 percent. Gains stalled early on workflow snags, then jumped when a single user-designed form and game-like incentives arrived. Focus groups showed resistance melting into routine use, though image archiving problems persisted. The authors credit user-led design and peer engagement.
pmc-13267039:
Ting Wang and colleagues present a 2026 cell study on a gum disease bacterium and liver cancer growth. The bacterium, Porphyromonas gingivalis, is known for gum infection but has been linked to wider disease. The team also tested carnosic acid, a compound from herbs, for any power to slow cancer cell growth.

The bacterium sped growth in one liver cancer cell line and in pancreatic cancer cells. It raised activity in growth and inflammation pathways inside the cells. Its outer toxin also boosted growth, and carnosic acid did not block that effect. In a second liver cell line, carnosic acid did slow growth, linked to a protective pathway. Effects thus depended on the cell type used.
pmc-13267939:
Maojiang Lyu and colleagues present a 2026 case report on rebuilding a teenager's thigh bone after infection. Their patient was a 14-year-old girl whose right thigh bone broke in a car crash. A pin-site infection led to chronic bone infection and a dead, unhealed segment. About eleven centimeters of bone had to be removed.

Care followed the induced membrane method, done in two stages. First, surgeons cleaned out the infection, fixed the bone with a rod, and placed antibiotic cement where bone was missing. Nearly three months later they removed the cement and packed the space with the girl's own bone graft. Six months after the second stage she bore full weight, lived normally, and showed healed bone with no return of infection.
pmc-13268139:
Taotao Peng and colleagues wrote a 2026 study of blood magnesium and lung harm in sepsis that starts outside the lungs. Sepsis is a runaway body response to infection. Lung complications are its deadliest turn. Using the MIMIC-IV intensive care database, the team studied 4,836 patients whose sepsis began outside the lungs and asked how starting magnesium levels related to lung complications.

Patients who developed lung complications died within 90 days far more often than those who did not. The link between magnesium and lung risk formed a U shape: both low and high levels carried more risk. The lowest-risk band sat between the two turning points the team found. Patients in the highest magnesium quarter had the worst survival of all. The authors suggest checking magnesium early may help foresee lung trouble in sepsis care.
pmc-13268639:
Haoran Zhang and colleagues present a 2026 mapping review of DeepSeek in medicine. DeepSeek is an open-source large language model, cheaper and easier to adapt than closed rivals. The team searched three databases for work from January to November 2025. They mapped 371 papers and reviewed 353 original articles in depth.

Output grew steadily, led by China, Turkey, and the United States. Uses covered patient teaching, decision support, training, workflow, and research. Results were often as good as rival models, with strengths in clear writing, some diagnosis tasks, low cost, and local use. Weak points included uneven results across fields, made-up content, and privacy and rule gaps. Two-thirds of the evidence was low quality, mostly untested benchmarks and fake cases. No trials measured real patient outcomes. The authors urge live testing before clinical use.
pmc-13269839:
Mingming Hu and co-authors published a trial report in 2026 on immune therapy plus chemotherapy around surgery for stage IIB to IIIB lung squamous cell cancer. Patients got two cycles of the immune drug camrelizumab with two chemotherapy drugs before surgery. The immune drug then continued for a year after surgery.

Forty-five patients were treated, and 41 reached surgery. Sixty percent achieved a major tumor response in the removed tissue, and 44.4 percent had no cancer left in it. At three years, 65.9 percent were disease-free and 68.7 percent were alive. Blood measures and smoking history were linked to major response. Certain immune cell gene patterns also differed between full and partial responders. The authors back the combined approach.
pmc-13270339:
Li Yuhong and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 presenting a method to measure carbon isotope ratios in airborne volatile organic compounds, gases that help form ozone and particles. Isotope fingerprints can reveal where the gases came from. Their method chains a heat-release sampler to separation and isotope instruments.

Seven compounds were validated, including benzene, toluene, and styrene. Best sampler settings were 300 degrees for five minutes. Precision was high, samples stayed stable for up to 50 days, and field air sampling worked well. Applied to ambient air, isotope signatures pointed mainly to traffic emissions. Only seven compounds are covered so far, a limit the authors flag for future work.
pmc-13271139:
Sho Nakamura is lead author of a 2026 journal article comparing self-measured eye pressure with professional measurement in Japanese patients with open-angle glaucoma. Eye pressure matters in glaucoma care, and a home device, the iCare HOME2, lets trained patients measure it sitting and lying down.

Thirty-six eyes from 36 patients were tested with a standard clinic method, a professional rebound device, and the home device, then retested after ten minutes lying flat. Lying pressures matched almost exactly between the professional and home devices, with very strong agreement, and sitting agreement was also strong with only small average differences. The authors say trained patients' home readings, in both positions, are reliable for clinical decisions.
pmc-13271439:
Sneha Vidyasagar is lead author of a 2026 retrospective study of calcitonin, a hormone drug, as an extra treatment for phantom limb pain after lower leg amputation. Phantom pain, felt in a limb that is no longer there, is hard to treat, so the team reviewed records of patients given at least three days of calcitonin.

The study covered 35 patients treated between 2017 and 2023, average age about 57, most with below-knee amputations for vascular disease, diabetic foot infection, or trauma. From the day before treatment to day seven, average pain intensity fell from 6.41 to 5.24, pain distress fell from 5.85 to 4.81, and reported relief rose. Daily morphine-equivalent dose did not change clearly.
pmc-13272239:
Jonas Henn is lead author of a 2026 journal article on making machine learning interpretable, understandable to clinicians, in emergency surgery for acute abdominal pain. Algorithms might help decide who needs urgent surgery. But doctors resist tools whose reasoning is hidden. So the team built a random-forest model. They tracked which features mattered at each stage of assessment.

Among 1,350 emergency patients, 276, or 20.4 percent, had urgent surgery within 24 hours. Model accuracy rose stepwise as data were added, from 0.53 with basic data to 0.83 after laboratory tests and physical examination. CT scanning added almost nothing at population level. Importance shifted from symptoms to vital signs, then to laboratory markers such as inflammation and clotting measures, plus abdominal guarding.
pmc-13273439:
Fei Wang leads a 2026 illustrative case of three separate primary brain tumors arising in sequence in one woman, without any radiation exposure. It calls on all member states to support international efforts against such acquisition. It calls on them to consider joining that convention. It calls on them to strengthen national controls over weapons, delivery systems, and related materials and technology.

Resolution 72/239 of the General Assembly, adopted at the seventy-second session, proclaims 2019 to 2028 as the United Nations Decade of Family Farming. It builds on the International Year of Family Farming held in 2014 and on the national committees and policies that year produced.

The text stresses that family farms produce more than 80 per cent of the world's food by value. Some 815 million people still suffer hunger. Most of the extreme poor live in rural areas. It encourages states to develop and share public policies that support family farmers, especially smallholders and women. It puts the Food and Agriculture Organization and the International Fund for Agricultural Development in charge of leading the Decade. Progress is reported to the Assembly every two years.
un-sc-res-1039:
Lebanon's interim force was renewed by the Security Council on 29 January 1996. The Secretary-General had reported on the United Nations Interim Force in Lebanon on 22 January. Lebanon's permanent representative had written on 17 January, and the government asked for the extension. The force's terms of reference went back to resolutions 425 and 426 (1978).

The Council extended UNIFIL's mandate for six months, to 31 July 1996. It restated its strong support for Lebanon's territorial integrity, sovereignty, and independence within its recognized borders. All parties were told to cooperate fully so the force could carry out its mandate in full. The Council condemned all acts of violence, above all those aimed at the force, and urged the parties to end them. It welcomed the streamlining of the force due by May 1996 and pressed for more savings in support services, as long as its working capacity stayed intact.
un-sc-res-1239:
Kosovo's refugee catastrophe drew a humanitarian appeal on 14 May 1999. Hundreds of thousands of Kosovo Albanians had fled into Albania, Macedonia, and Bosnia. More were displaced inside Kosovo and Montenegro. The refugee agency and relief groups strained to feed and shelter them. The Secretary-General planned a needs assessment mission to the region.

The Council praised the states and relief organizations already helping the refugees. It urged all who could to give more resources for the relief effort. It called for access for the United Nations and all humanitarian staff working in Kosovo and other parts of Yugoslavia. The right of every refugee and displaced person to return home in safety and dignity was reaffirmed. The Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was pressed to let aid reach the displaced and to work toward a political settlement. The text stopped short of the force questions the Council would face in June.
un-sc-res-1339:
Georgia's observer mission was kept on as the Abkhazia talks stalled on 31 January 2001. The Secretary-General's report of 18 January lay before the Council. The zone of conflict stayed mostly calm but volatile. The two sides had met in their coordinating council on 23 January. UNOMIG and the CIS peacekeeping force worked closely together.

The Council extended UNOMIG's mandate for a period ending 31 July 2001. The extension could be reviewed if the CIS force changed. The Council backed the special representative's plan to table a draft paper on dividing powers between Tbilisi and Sukhumi. Work on a protocol for refugee returns to the Gali region had to speed up. The Abkhaz side in particular was called to end its refusal to negotiate the core issues. The Council restated that the population shifts caused by the conflict were unacceptable and that all refugees held the right to return home.
un-sc-res-139: The Federation of Mali sought a seat at the United Nations in 1960. On 28 June 1960 the Security Council examined its application. It recommended to the General Assembly that the federation be admitted to membership. The vote was unanimous, and the text is a single sentence long. The federation joined weeks later. It broke apart soon after, and Mali and Senegal entered as separate states.
un-sc-res-1439:
Angola's peace held while the Council finished the UNITA sanctions story on 24 October 2002. The government and UNITA were applying the peace accords and the April 2002 memorandum that ended the war. The Joint Commission had met again, and a United Nations Mission in Angola had been set up. The Council still voiced concern at the war's humanitarian toll on civilians.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extended the UNITA monitoring mechanism for two months, to 19 December 2002. Two experts would be named to serve on it. The mechanism owed the sanctions committee a report by 13 December, focused on sanctions breaches. All states were called to cooperate with it fully. The Council also ended parts of resolution 1127 (1997), the travel measures on UNITA, from 1 November 2002. The step marked the sanctions regime winding down as the peace took hold.
un-sc-res-1539:
Children forced into war stand at the center of Resolution 1539, adopted in April 2004. Armed groups in several conflicts were recruiting boys and girls as fighters and servants. The Council condemned the practice and demanded action plans from listed parties to end it.

Inside, the members threaten measures against groups that keep using child soldiers and ask for a worldwide monitoring system to name violators. The text built toward the UN's later formal watch list for child recruitment. For readers, it marks the point where protecting children in war became a standing Council duty, not a passing concern.
un-sc-res-1639: Security Council Resolution 1639 is held here as a Wikisource transcription of the United Nations official record. Its form is standard and deliberate: situation first, judgment second, action third. Because later disputes often turn on what exactly was decided, preserving the whole text, rather than a summary, is the service this entry performs.
un-sc-res-1739:
Côte d'Ivoire is the subject of United Nations Security Council Resolution 1739, adopted on 10 January 2007. The country stayed split after civil war, and the crisis kept getting worse. Civilians suffered and many fled their homes. Elections were planned by 31 October 2007 under a transition plan.

The text extends the United Nations Operation in Côte d'Ivoire and the French forces backing it until 30 June 2007. It restates the mission's full task list in detail. The tasks cover watching the cease-fire, disarming fighters and militias, guarding voter registration, and policing the arms embargo. The mission may use all necessary means, and French forces may step in to protect civilians and support the operation.
un-sc-res-1939: Resolution 1939 is one of the Security Council's formal acts, preserved in official wording through a Wikisource transcription. The document was written for immediate use by governments and UN officials, in language tested for agreement among fifteen delegations. That tested language is the entry, kept whole so its precision can still do its work.
un-sc-res-239:
Foreign mercenaries were fighting in the Congo again in 1967. The Congolese government had sent the Council a message on the threat. On 10 July 1967 the Council debated the danger to the Congo's independence. It restated its 1966 rule against outside interference. Mercenary bands had seized towns in the east that month. Their presence drove the emergency tone of the text.

Any state that lets mercenaries be recruited for overthrowing governments stands condemned. Governments must keep their land and their nationals out of such plots. Training, transit, and planning for mercenaries all had to be blocked. The target was the overthrow of the Congo's government. The Council stayed seized of the question.
un-sc-res-339: United Nations record keeping gives this text the number 339, and the catalog dates it 1973. Resolutions are the way the Council states its decisions, and member states are expected to take them seriously. Preserving the text in this form keeps a small piece of diplomatic history open to any reader. Its place here reflects the library's aim of keeping primary records readable.
un-sc-res-39:
Kashmir's war brought India and Pakistan before the Security Council within months of their freedom. Resolution 39, passed on 20 January 1948, holds that the state of affairs between the two new states needs study as a matter of haste. Left to run, the fight could put world peace and safety at risk. The Council acts under its power to probe any dispute of that kind.

A Commission of the Security Council is set up, of three members. India picks one, Pakistan picks one, and the two so picked name the third. The team must go to the spot as fast as it can. It acts under the Council's sway and must keep the Council told of its work in full. The team grew into the long UN watch over Kashmir.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Resolution 1039, passed on 29 January 1996, keeps the UN force in south Lebanon for six more months. The force, UNIFIL, had been there since 1978. A UN report of 22 January set out its recent work. Lebanon's envoy had asked in a letter for more time, and the Council granted the request.

The term now ran to 31 July 1996. The Council restated its strong backing for Lebanon's unity and freedom, inside borders the world accepts. It set out the force's tasks once more, as first drawn in 1978. All sides were told to work with the force in full, so it could do its job. Calm in the south served no one if the force stood blocked.

Resolution 1239, adopted on 14 May 1999, addresses the refugee catastrophe produced by the Kosovo crisis. Enormous numbers of Kosovar Albanians had fled into Albania, Macedonia, Bosnia, and beyond, while displacement inside Kosovo and other parts of Yugoslavia kept climbing. The Council grounded its concern in human rights law, refugee law, and the Geneva Conventions.

It demanded that aid agencies and the UN refugee agency be given safe, unimpeded access to Kosovo and the rest of Yugoslavia so help could reach people in need. It stressed coordinating relief among states and relief organizations, and it backed the right of all refugees and displaced people to return home safely. A UN humanitarian assessment mission to the region was also welcomed.

Georgia's frozen conflict in Abkhazia fills Resolution 1339, adopted unanimously on 31 January 2001. The Council called the continued lack of progress on a comprehensive settlement unacceptable. The zone was mostly calm, it noted, but the general situation remained very volatile, and the two sides' coordinating council had met just days earlier.

The mandate of the UN observer mission in Georgia, UNOMIG, was extended for six months, to July 2001. The Council stressed how closely the observers and the Commonwealth of Independent States peacekeeping force worked together on the ground. It welcomed their stabilizing contribution while making clear that observation was no substitute for a political deal on Abkhazia's status.

A union that lived for weeks still left its trace at the UN. On 28 June 1960, the Council adopted Resolution 139 without dissent. The applicant was the Federation of Mali. Senegal and the Sudanese Republic had formed it as French West Africa broke up. France had just granted the union its freedom, days before.

Having weighed the bid, the Council urges the Assembly to admit the federation. The union broke apart that August, before the Assembly met. The story then ran on through two more texts in this series. One seated the Republic of Mali, the other Senegal. Each state entered on its own in the end.

Resolution 1439, adopted unanimously on 24 October 2002, manages the tail end of sanctions against Angola's UNITA movement. Angola's long civil war had ended that April, months after UNITA leader Jonas Savimbi was killed, and the government and UNITA were carrying out their peace accords. A joint commission had reconvened, and a new UN mission in Angola had been created to support the settlement.

With that progress noted, the Council kept the sanctions monitoring machinery in place for a short final stretch, judging that watching compliance still mattered while peace took hold. It also voiced concern for civilians suffering the war's humanitarian effects. Angola's sanctions regime, once a centerpiece of Council action, was being wound down.

Child soldiers and other abuses against children in war are tackled on 22 April 2004. Earlier resolutions had built a framework of rules and lists of offending parties. Yet parties to conflicts still violated children's rights with impunity, the Council says, and little had changed on the ground.

Listed parties are demanded to produce action plans to stop recruiting and using children, with a warning of measures against those who refuse. The Secretary-General is asked to design, within three months, a full monitoring and reporting system on child soldier recruitment and other grave abuses. That system would draw on United Nations agencies, governments, regional bodies, and civic groups for timely and reliable information.

Bosnia and Herzegovina's European Union stabilization force is renewed on 21 November 2005 for a further planned period. The force had taken over from NATO's SFOR the year before. Full support is again voiced for the High Representative and for completing the 1995 peace agreement.

Acting under Chapter VII, states working through the European Union are authorized to keep the force in place under unified command. They may take all necessary measures to carry out the military terms of the peace agreement and to defend the force and help it complete its mission. The parties are told to respect the force's safety and freedom of movement, and the authorization would be reviewed as the peace required.

UNOCI's mandate is restated in full by Resolution 1739, adopted on 10 January 2007. Côte d'Ivoire's crisis persisted, with grave humanitarian effects, and elections were due by 31 October 2007 under the transition plan in Resolution 1721 (2006). The UN Operation in Côte d'Ivoire and the French forces backing it were the core of the international presence.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extends both mandates until 30 June 2007. UNOCI's tasks are to watch the ceasefire, help disarm and demobilize fighters, dismantle militias, and secure voter identification and registration. They also cover protecting civilians under imminent threat, monitoring the arms embargo, supporting humanitarian access, helping restore state authority nationwide, and backing free elections with logistics and security. The French forces are authorized to use all necessary means in support, including protecting civilians in their areas. A review of mandate length and troop levels is promised by June 2007.

Nepal was working through a peace process after its long civil war when the Council adopted Resolution 1939 in 2010. The former Maoist rebels had joined politics under the peace agreement of 2006. The United Nations Mission in Nepal, called UNMIN, watched the arms and fighters of both sides.

The Council renewed UNMIN's mandate until 15 January 2011. It decided that the mission would then leave Nepal for good. Both the government and the Maoists had asked for that end date. Nepal's parties were pressed to finish the peace process by then. The hardest question was what would happen to the Maoist fighters. They had to join the security forces or return to civilian life. Work on a new constitution was also still unfinished.

Mercenaries, not Cyprus, drive Resolution 239. Foreign soldiers of fortune were fighting in the Congo again in 1967. White mercenaries had seized towns in the east. The Congolese government sent the Council an urgent message. Resolution 239 was adopted unanimously on 10 July 1967.

Members reaffirmed their 1966 demand on the Congo. They condemned any state still letting mercenaries be recruited. Governments had to police their own soil and citizens. No planning, training, or transit of mercenaries aimed at Congo's government would be tolerated. The Secretary-General had to track compliance closely. The text is an early landmark in the UN's long campaign against mercenary warfare in Africa.

The October war of 1973 was still burning when the Council adopted Resolution 339 on 23 October. Resolution 338, passed the day before, had ordered a cease-fire between Israel and its Arab neighbors. The fighting had not stopped in time. More had to be done to make the order real.

The Council confirmed its decision of the day before. All firing and all military action had to stop at once. The forces of the two sides were urged to return to their earlier positions. Those were the positions they held when the cease-fire was due to take effect. The Secretary-General was asked to send United Nations observers at once. They would watch over the cease-fire between Israel and Egypt. The observers would come from United Nations personnel already in the Middle East, above all in the Suez Canal area.

India and Pakistan, two brand-new states, were already in conflict over Jammu and Kashmir at the start of 1948. The princely state's future was the core of the dispute. Resolution 39, adopted on 20 January 1948, set up a United Nations commission for the dispute.

The commission had three members. India would pick one, Pakistan would pick one, and those two would name the third. The commission was sent to the area with a double job. It had to investigate the facts, under Article 34 of the Charter. It also had to act as a mediator between the parties, without slowing down the investigation. It could travel wherever its work required. Decisions would be taken by majority vote, and the Council would supply staff and help.

A small state on Europe's edge won its freedom in August 1991. It had been a Soviet republic. Now it sought a seat of its own at the UN. War clouds hung over its eastern strip, where rebels rejected the new state. Resolution 739 was passed without a vote on 5 February 1992.

The Council backed the bid from the Republic of Moldova. It told the General Assembly to admit the country. The Assembly did so in March 1992. The seat confirmed Moldova's borders in the eyes of the world. That point gained weight weeks later. Fights in the east flared into a short war. The clash froze into a dispute that still lasts.
villa-rubein-and-other-stories-pg2639: John Galsworthy's Villa Rubein and other stories: early tales of love and society. The Forsyte author's apprentice work, sensitive and refined. A fine collection. Galsworthy's early stories show the master forming, the master forming, sensitive and refined.
weddynge-syr-gawen-dame-ragnell-madden-1:
The Weddynge of Syr Gawen and Dame Ragnell is a Middle English romance edited by Frederic Madden in 1839. It tells the famous loathly lady tale. A threatening knight spares King Arthur's life on one condition, and Gawain must pay the price.

Arthur must learn within a year what women most desire. The hideous Dame Ragnell knows the answer, and she will trade it for marriage to Gawain. He agrees, for the king's sake, and treats his bride with full courtesy. On the wedding night her ugliness falls away. The answer, that women want rule over their own lives, is the tale's lasting point.
